A friend of mine worked through a major disappointment by painting; as he poured his pain onto the canvas, he expressed himself and ended up creating beautiful work. Another friend used to say that writing healed him. But someone else in the same situation might go maladaptive—displacing their anger by yelling at the first driver who cuts them off in traffic or snapping at whoever feels safe to target. It releases tension for an instant, but it doesn’t solve anything and only further damages relationships and peace of mind. In the end, defense mechanisms are neither purely protective knights nor cruel dungeon masters. They take shape based on how much authority we give them. If we use them with awareness—knowing why we’re building that wall—they keep us standing. But if we hand over the reins and let them run on autopilot, we get lost in Freud’s complex theories and watch helplessly as the many-headed monster Anna described devours us piece by piece. So how do we build that awareness? The first step is simple: observe our defense mechanisms without judgment. When we start raising a wall, pause and ask: “Is this wall really protecting me from what’s outside, or is it imprisoning my own feelings?” Trying to name the mechanism out loud—or on paper—is already a crack in the wall. Maybe not enough to walk through. But enough to remember the door exists. It’s also possible to consciously shift toward adaptive mechanisms: channeling anger into sublimation instead of repression, bringing in humor, or embracing Beckett’s “fail better” mindset to crack the door open a little. While we still hold the key to our own dungeon, stepping outside occasionally—despite all the lunatics out there—to take a clean breath of air is far better than rotting behind the walls we built ourselves. And as long as the key is in our hand, it’s entirely possible to relieve that inner “dungeon master” of its duties.

title: Will AI Be Enough for Us?
description: A Reflection on AI’s Promise and the Warmth It Can’t Replicate
text: AI agents haven’t fully entered our lives yet—I know that. Most of us still wake up and go about our day without talking to an assistant, relying purely on our own will. But then again, which of us hasn’t turned to an AI for a quick email, a tricky presentation title, or just to say, “Take a look at this”? Sometimes, this worries me. It feels like we’re walking a thin, invisible tightrope between surrendering to AI and using it as a mind-expanding helper—perhaps even a friend. I was recently talking to a friend who is a university professor. He laughed and said something quite strange: “Hakan, it’s reached a point where students are having AI write their essays, and I’m sitting there having AI read them.” Isn’t that surreal? One machine writes, another machine reads, and we pretend an education is happening in between. Perhaps this is an inevitable part of the transition we’re in. Naturally, we prefer whatever makes our work easier. But before we find ourselves standing in a sudden, vast void, unsure of what to do next, we need to talk about this—for the sake of conversation itself. Could this void I’m talking about be the absence of human effort? Those painful moments when we used to pause to fix a sentence, delete and rewrite, or rack our brains for the perfect word… Were those moments just a waste of time? Or were they the very necessities that make us who we are—the friction that allows our thoughts to cook and mature? If we outsource that process—the jagged, unbalanced, and rugged path of thinking—to machines, will the flawless, sterile result truly satisfy us? More importantly, when we stop enduring that struggle, are we quietly surrendering our ability to be self-sufficient? And what about the bonds we form while supporting each other through hard times? If we solve every problem with a single command, will we stop needing one another? If we deem those bonds unnecessary and let them fray, will we cross a line from which there is no return? I’m not sure. But I think part of the answer lies in realizing that the “it’s too hard, let someone else do it” mindset isn’t always our friend. Because being self-sufficient means choosing to do some things ourselves—even if technology could do them better—simply because it feels good, because we love the walk along that difficult path. Perhaps in the future, our greatest joy will be saying, “No, stop,” and then, “I want to feel this, I want to solve this, I want to experience this myself.” Because life is about who we fall with and whose hand we hold to get back up. And I fear no algorithm will ever be able to replicate the warmth of a hand reached out when you hit the ground. I had a friend who valued self-sufficiency above all else. He never wanted help with anything; no matter how hard it was, he did it himself. When he finally bought the house he’d dreamed of since childhood, he refused our help even with the move. “By doing this, you’re taking away the moments we could have shared,” I told him. “We could meet in the morning, finish the heavy lifting together, and then head to the seaside to eat and share a glass of rakı. You’re robbing us of these memories just to avoid being a burden by saying, ‘No need, I’ll handle it.’ Those moments would have been memories now. We have many beautiful memories together, but they are limited. We missed those times of helping each other and celebrating the result together.” I lost that friend two years ago. I still miss him dearly. Today, technology whispers the exact same sentence into our ears: “No need, don’t tire yourself, I’ll handle it.” While this promise feels like ultimate comfort, I can see the desolation behind it more clearly now. That’s why, no matter how much AI eases our lives, we must stubbornly insist on choosing the difficult path sometimes. We will remember the moments we stood shoulder to shoulder, got tired, perhaps made mistakes, but then sat down to celebrate—moments that were truly ours.

title: Why Do We Say Hello?
description: Transactional Analysis and the Hidden Games in Our Relationships
text:
Have you ever found yourself in an argument you never intended to have, asking, “How did we even get here?” Or, despite being an adult, have you ever felt yourself suddenly shrinking into a guilty child in front of an authority figure? Often, communication breaks down because hidden parts of us take the wheel while we speak.

Completed by Eric Berne in just two years, Transactional Analysis, or TA, offers us a map of human psychology to make sense of these internal dynamics and the invisible layers of communication. Developed in the 1950s, this approach grew out of his detailed studies on how individuals project themselves and engage with those around them. It focuses on the active exchange between people to decode the underlying patterns of their behavior.

It helps us discover the hidden corners of our inner world and bridge the gap between who we are and the world around us.

The Mind Behind TA

Born in Montréal, Canada in 1910, Dr. Eric Berne was a psychiatrist and a polymath who received education in various fields alongside his medical training.

In addition to medicine, he pursued studies in literature, public relations, and anthropology. This diverse background enriched his perspective and greatly influenced his development of TA.

A Simple “Hello”

In the business world, a transaction refers to a simple exchange process. However, when Berne applied this to social life, it took on a much deeper meaning. According to him, every greeting and every glance is a spiritual exchange. This leads to a simple question: Why do we say “Hello” in the first place?

According to Berne, the answer to this is recognition hunger, which is just as vital as physical hunger. Just as our bodies need food to survive, our souls need stimuli to feel that they exist. Berne named every unit of attention that satisfies this hunger a stroke.

For us, the greatest fear is being ignored. Therefore, if we cannot attract positive attention, we seek a negative reaction just to prove our existence. Think of a child who knowingly makes their mother angry by being naughty. They willingly accept being scolded, as her shouting is far more bearable than her indifferent silence. Because receiving a reaction, no matter how negative, is the most concrete proof of saying I am here and I exist. I think I can also give the example of my cat trying to bite my foot out of nowhere when I haven’t paid attention to him for a while.

To understand this, we need to meet the three characters inside us that struggle to take control.

The Four Key Tools of Transactional Analysis

Structural Analysis explores the architecture of our personality. It answers the question: Who is really speaking right now? The Parent, the Adult, or the Child?

Transactional Analysis Proper examines the flow of communication between people. It looks at whether we are really understanding each other, or if we are entirely disconnected.

Game Analysis reveals the hidden patterns in our relationships. It explains why we keep falling into the same conflicts and repetitive emotional traps to gain attention.

Life Script Analysis focuses on the unconscious life plan we wrote for ourselves in childhood. It shows how yesterday’s decisions limit today’s freedom.

Structural Analysis

Ego States: The Three Voices Inside

An ego state is a consistent set of feelings, thoughts, and related behaviors. We switch between three distinct ego states constantly, and use them to interact with the outside world or to hold conversations—sometimes endless ones while staring at the ceiling in bed—with ourselves. While inspired by Freud’s psychoanalytic model, these states functionally categorize a person’s internal world:

  • Child Ego State—The present-day manifestation of the emotions, thoughts, and behavior patterns a person experienced as a child.
  • Adult Ego State—The part of the person that evaluates internal and external reality as it is in the “here and now,” processes data, and responds logically.
  • Parent Ego State—A reflection of the values, rules, and behaviors of the parents or other authority figures that the person has internalized since childhood.

Parent Ego State

The Parent Ego State encompasses the attitudes and behaviors learned and copied from the parents and other role models. Think about the significant people from your past. It could be your mother, father, older siblings or your teachers—anyone who was important to you. Those are the people who have positively and negatively influenced your life. Your Parent Ego State contains all these people. At any given moment, you can go into thinking, feeling and acting like one of them.

Adult Ego State

The Adult Ego State emerges around six months in the child. It always functions in the present, and processes our thoughts and feelings rationally. In this state, we are aware of ourselves, our impact on others, and take account what is going on around us. In other words, it’s us being our true selves, free from external influences of our Parent and Child Ego States.

Child Ego State

Generally speaking, when we are being selfish, affectionate, playful, creative, mean, or are simply having fun, we are operating from our Child Ego State. We are in our Child Ego State when we think, feel, and behave in the same way we did when we were children. In many ways, it is one of the most important parts of our personality because both creativity and curiosity come from the child in us.

“Creating a harmonious relationship between the ego states is one of the most effective ways of being more mindful, staying in the moment and enjoying life more.”

Reading Between the Lines: The Hidden Layers of Talk

Transactional analysis proper examines how people actually communicate through three main types of transactions: complementary, crossed, and ulterior.

Complementary Transactions: When the response matches the ego state that was addressed, the transaction is called complementary. In such cases, communication usually flows smoothly and can continue for a long time without conflict.

Crossed Transactions: A crossed transaction occurs when the response comes from a different ego state than the one that was expected. This mismatch often causes confusion, frustration, or a sudden breakdown in communication.

Ulterior Transactions: According to Berne, communication often happens on two levels at once—the obvious social message and a hidden psychological message underneath. People usually sense the hidden layer, even if they can’t clearly explain why they feel uncomfortable.

Life Script: The Unconscious Blueprint

One of the central concepts in TA is the life script. Essentially, this is a life plan that we wrote for ourselves when we were just children without even realizing it.

As kids, we try to make sense of the world. Based on the messages we get from our parents or from the people we consider significant, we create a ‘survival guide’ to secure our place in the world. Back then, these decisions were vital strategies.

The tragedy begins in adulthood. Even though the years pass and the stage changes, we stick to that old script. Even if it limits us, we stubbornly continue to play out the specific role we wrote as children.

For instance, many boys around the world might decide early in life that it’s unsafe to express emotions like crying. This decision might be reinforced by their parental figures, leading them to have difficulties in connecting with emotions as adults in the present.

Games People Play

Berne observed that human interactions often follow specific, recurring patterns he called games. This concept became the foundation of his 1964 bestseller, “Games People Play,” a work that remains influential today. In TA, a game always involves an ulterior motive—usually a subconscious quest for recognition or validation—which operates beneath the surface.

To be classified as a game, the interaction must meet specific criteria:

  • It follows a repetitive pattern.
  • It occurs outside of Adult awareness.
  • The true message is conveyed at the psychological level.
  • It always results in a hidden payoff for the players.
  • It concludes with a familiar, often negative emotion known as a racket feeling.

“Why don’t you…? Yes, but…”

Imagine a scenario where someone named Blue complains about a lack of energy.

Blue: I feel exhausted all the time. I really need to get back in shape.

Green: Why don’t you join the gym down the street?

Blue: Yes, but it is too expensive for me right now.

Green: Well, why don’t you go for a run in the park?

Blue: Yes, but my knees hurt when I run on hard pavement.

Green: Why don’t you try swimming then?

Blue: Yes, but the pool is always crowded when I get off work.

Eventually, Green runs out of ideas. On the surface, this appears to be a constructive conversation. However, underneath, Blue is playing a game to prove that the problem is unsolvable. Blue rejects every solution to leave Green feeling helpless, and confirms the hidden belief that nothing will work.

Breaking Free: The Power to Choose

The ultimate objective of TA is to empower the Adult Ego State. By developing a conscious understanding of our psychological games and life scripts, we gain the ability to make more intentional choices. This awareness allows us to detach from the weight of past traumas and the pressure of future anxieties. Ultimately, TA provides the framework we need to view our relationships and what is happening around us with greater mindfulness and clarity across all areas of life.

title: bosh
description: Bosh, nonsense or empty talk, comes from the Turkish boş, meaning empty. It became current in English through J. J. Morier’s 1834 novel Ayesha, the Maid of Kars.
text: Bosh means nonsense or empty talk in English. It comes from the Turkish word boş , meaning empty. 1 It became current in English in the nineteenth century through J. J. Morier’s 1834 novel Ayesha, the Maid of Kars . What was empty in Turkish became empty talk in English, and then nonsense. 1 2 It is old-fashioned now, but it is still there. You’re talking bosh.

title: influence
description: Influence was once a fluid: medieval Latin influentia, a flowing in from the stars. Influenza is the same word, and flu is what is left of it.
text: Influence means the power to affect someone or something. It comes from the medieval Latin influentia , a flowing in, from influere , to flow in. 1 In the Middle Ages, influence was believed to be a fluid that streamed down from the stars into people and shaped their character and their fortune. 1 Influenza is the same word. It is simply the Italian for influence, and epidemics were once blamed on the stars. Flu is what is left of it. 1 He was under the influence.

title: quarantine
description: Quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta, forty. In 1920 Russian refugees were kept in quarantine off İstanbul.
text: Quarantine is a period of separation that keeps a disease from spreading. It comes from the Italian quaranta , forty. 1 During the plague, ships arriving from infected places could be kept at anchor for forty days before anyone came ashore. The Italian for forty is quaranta . The period became quarantena . 1 In 1920, ships carrying Russians who had fled the civil war were kept in quarantine off İstanbul before their passengers were allowed to land. Typhus was one of the main fears. Some later accounts say forty days, but contemporary memoirs and recent scholarship describe quarantines lasting from a few days to two weeks. I could not confirm forty days for the 1920 arrivals. 2 3 A quarantine is rarely forty days now. It is ten days, or two weeks, or whatever the illness needs. The forty is still in the word. The ship was held in quarantine.

title: nightmare
description: The mare in nightmare is an old word for a spirit or demon believed to trouble sleepers. The horse is a different word.
text: A nightmare is a bad dream. The mare in it is an old word for a spirit or demon once believed to trouble sleeping people. The horse is a different word. 1 2 In the old belief, the mare oppressed the sleeper and brought a feeling of suffocation. The word later moved from the creature to the experience, and then to a frightening dream. 2 The creature disappeared from belief, but the word stayed. Related forms survive in other Germanic languages too. 2 It was a nightmare.

title: Rosetta stone
description: The Rosetta Stone gave scholars the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs. The name now means any clue that makes a difficult mystery possible to understand.
text: A Rosetta stone is a clue or discovery that makes a difficult mystery possible to understand. The original Rosetta Stone was found in Egypt in 1799. The same decree had been written on it in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Ancient Greek. Scholars could read the Greek. For the first time, they had a way to compare a known text with writing they could not yet read. 1 Thomas Young made important early advances. In 1822, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion made the decisive breakthrough and showed that hieroglyphs could record the sounds of the Egyptian language. 1 A replica stands in the NSA’s National Cryptologic Museum, in an exhibit on the work of the agency’s language analysts. 2 The new evidence proved to be a Rosetta stone.

title: broadcast
description: Before broadcast meant radio or television, it described seed scattered by hand over a wide area.
text: To broadcast something is to send it out to many people. The word was used first for scattering seed over a wide area, usually by hand. That agricultural sense is much older than radio. 1 2 In the early twentieth century, broadcast was taken up for radio transmission. The older idea of sending something out widely was kept, but the seed had become a signal. 2 The agricultural meaning still exists today. 1 The interview was broadcast live.

title: boycott
description: Boycott comes from Charles Boycott, an English land agent in Ireland whose name became the term for organized refusal and social exclusion.
text: To boycott something is to refuse to buy, use, or take part in it as a form of protest. The word comes from Charles Boycott, an English land agent in County Mayo, Ireland. In 1880, during a dispute over rents and evictions, local people and members of the Irish Land League isolated him. Workers left, businesses refused to deal with him, and his name became attached to the tactic. 1 2 The name spread quickly from one dispute to a general word for organized refusal. 1 2 They agreed to boycott the company.

title: maverick
description: Maverick first referred to unbranded cattle associated with Samuel Maverick. It later became a word for an independent person.
text: A maverick is an independent person who does not follow the group. The word comes from Samuel A. Maverick, a nineteenth-century Texas landowner. Unbranded cattle associated with him came to be called mavericks , and the word spread through cattle country for unbranded animals. 1 2 By the end of the nineteenth century, the word was also being used for people who went their own way. 1 2 She was a maverick in her field.

title: guy
description: Guy comes from Guy Fawkes. His name passed to effigies, then to strangely dressed men, and eventually to an everyday word for a person.
text: A guy is an ordinary word for a man or, in some uses, a person. The word comes from Guy Fawkes. Effigies of him burned on November 5 came to be called guys . The word then spread to people who looked strange or badly dressed. 1 2 In American English, guy became a general word for a man, and the plural guys later widened further in everyday speech. 1 2 He seems like a nice guy.

title: deadline
description: During the American Civil War, a dead line was a prison boundary prisoners were forbidden to cross. The modern time-limit sense may have been influenced by it.
text: A deadline is the latest time by which something must be done. During the American Civil War, dead line was used for a boundary inside some military prisons. Prisoners were forbidden to cross it, and guards could fire on those who did. Andersonville is the best-known example, but the National Park Service notes that such lines were used at several prisons. 1 The modern sense of a final time limit appeared in American newspaper jargon by 1919. The older prison use may have influenced it, but the connection is not certain. 2 The deadline is Friday.

title: algorithm
description: Algorithm ultimately comes from the name of the ninth-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose work on calculation reached Europe in Latin translation.
text: An algorithm is a set of steps for solving a problem or carrying out a calculation. The word ultimately comes from the name of the ninth-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi. A Latin version of a work associated with him on Hindu-Arabic numerals used a form of his name, Algoritmi . That name gave rise to algorism , a word for arithmetic using those numerals. 1 2 Over time, the spelling and meaning changed. Algorithm came to mean a defined procedure for calculation and then, more broadly, a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem. 1 2 The search engine uses an algorithm to rank results.

title: robot
description: Robot entered international use through Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R. The word was suggested by his brother Josef from Czech robota, meaning forced labour or hard work.
text: A robot is a machine that can carry out tasks automatically. The word entered international use through Karel Čapek’s 1920 play R.U.R. , where it named artificial workers. Čapek later credited his brother Josef with suggesting the word. 1 2 Josef drew it from Czech robota , a word connected with forced labour, serf labour, or hard work. The labour was already in the name before the modern machine existed. 1 2 The factory uses robots for welding.

title: candidate
description: Candidate comes from Latin candidatus, meaning white-robed. Roman men seeking public office were associated with a bright white toga.
text: A candidate is someone being considered for a position, office, award, or other selection. The word comes from Latin candidatus , meaning white-robed. In ancient Rome, a man seeking public office was associated with a bright white toga, and the word for the clothing became the word for the office-seeker. 1 2 English later widened candidate beyond elections to people being considered for many kinds of positions or outcomes. 1 She was one of three candidates for the position.

title: disaster
description: Disaster came through French from Italian disastro, built from a negative prefix and astro, star. One of its earliest senses concerned an unfavourable star or planet.
text: A disaster is a catastrophe or serious misfortune. The word came into English through French from Italian disastro . The second part comes from astro , star. One of the earliest English senses referred to an unfavourable influence or position of a star or planet. 1 2 The word then settled into the broader meaning of a great misfortune or catastrophe. The astrological belief disappeared from ordinary use, but it remains in the word’s history. 1 2 The storm became a disaster for the coastal towns.

title: companion
description: Companion comes through French from a Late Latin word formed from com-, together, and panis, bread: someone associated with sharing bread.
text: A companion is someone who goes with you or spends time with you. The word came through Old French from a Late Latin form built from com- , together, and panis , bread. Its older sense was a fellow or associate understood through the idea of sharing bread or a meal. 1 2 The meaning widened into the familiar sense of a person who accompanies another. The bread is no longer part of the definition, but it is part of the word’s construction. 1 2 She was his companion on the long journey.

title: desire
description: Desire comes from Latin desiderare, to long for or feel the absence of something. A connection with sidus, star, is possible, but the exact history is uncertain.
text: A desire is a feeling of wanting something. English got the word through Old French from Latin desiderare . In Latin, the verb could mean to long for something, but also to miss it or feel its absence. 1 2 There is a well-known explanation that connects desiderare with sidus , star or constellation. On that reading, the word may once have carried an idea connected with looking to the stars or waiting for what they would bring. 1 2 The exact origin is not certain. Etymologists have proposed other explanations too, so the neat claim that desire simply means something like “from the stars” goes further than the evidence allows. 2 What is secure is the older sense of longing for what is absent. He had a strong desire to go home.

title: consider
description: Consider comes from Latin considerare, to observe attentively or contemplate. It is probably connected with sidus, star or constellation, though the exact origin is not certain.
text: To consider something is to think about it carefully. The word comes through Old French from Latin considerare , to observe attentively or contemplate. 1 2 A long-standing explanation connects the Latin verb with sidus , meaning a star, heavenly body, or constellation. On that reading, considerare may once have meant something like observing the stars closely, perhaps for navigation or divination. 1 2 The connection is probable rather than certain. Other explanations for the Latin verb have been proposed, so the star story is best kept as a strong possibility rather than a literal definition. 2 English kept the idea of close attention even after the stars disappeared from ordinary use. I need some time to consider the offer.

title: kiosk
description: Kiosk came into English through French from the Turkish köşk, an open garden pavilion. The word has been getting smaller ever since.
text: A kiosk is a small stall you buy something at, or a screen you touch to print a ticket. It came into English through the French kiosque , from the Turkish köşk , and behind that the Persian kūshk . 1 A köşk was a pavilion, open on some or all sides, built in a garden to be sat in. The Çinili Köşk at Topkapı, put up in 1472 under Mehmed II, was a pleasure pavilion in the outer gardens, used to watch the games and spectacles held in the square it faced. 2 Europe borrowed the building first, in the seventeenth century, as ornament for parks and gardens. Then the word was handed down to smaller and smaller things: a newspaper stand by the 1860s, a telephone box in the 1920s, and now a machine bolted to the floor of an airport. 1 She bought a ticket at the kiosk.

title: noon
description: Noon comes from the Latin nona hora, the ninth hour, which fell around three in the afternoon. The hour moved and the nine stayed.
text: Noon is the middle of the day. The word comes from the Latin nona hora , the ninth hour, one of the fixed hours of prayer. 1 2 Counted from around six in the morning, the ninth hour fell at about three in the afternoon. That is where noon was in English for a long time. 1 2 Between the twelfth century and the fourteenth it moved to midday. Why is not settled. Unreliable clocks, daylight that stretches and shrinks with the northern seasons, and the fact that a day’s fast ended at nones have all been offered as reasons. 1 2 Noon settled at twelve and stayed there. The hour it is named after is three hours later. We’ll meet at noon.

title: curfew
description: Curfew comes from the Old French cuevrefeu, cover fire: an evening bell telling a town built of timber to bank its hearths for the night.
text: A curfew is an order to be off the streets after a certain hour. The word comes from the Old French cuevrefeu , cover fire. 1 In medieval towns built largely of timber, a bell rang in the evening and households banked or covered their hearths for the night. A fire left untended was everybody’s problem. 1 2 The cover itself was called a curfew too: a lid of terracotta or metal put over the embers to hold them safely until morning. 2 The bell stopped and the fire went out of the meaning. By the nineteenth century the word had become what it is now, an hour after which you have to be indoors. 1 The city was under curfew.

title: ostracism
description: Ostracism comes from ostrakon, a potsherd. Athenians voted to banish a man by scratching his name on a piece of broken pottery.
text: Ostracism is being shut out by the group you belong to. The word comes from the Greek ostrakon , a potsherd: a piece of broken pottery. 1 An Athenian who wanted a man banished for ten years scratched his name on a sherd and handed it in. Broken pottery was everywhere, which is why the vote was taken on it. 1 2 Thousands of those sherds have come out of the Agora and the Kerameikos, names still legible on them, most of them from refuse dumps. 2 The procedure ended and the word kept only the exclusion. The object dropped out of it: a piece of rubbish with a name scratched on it. 1 He faced ostracism from the whole village.

title: vaccine
description: Vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, cow. The first protection against smallpox was taken from cowpox, and the cow stayed in the name.
text: A vaccine is a preparation that trains the body against a disease. The word comes from the Latin vacca , cow. 1 2 Edward Jenner’s report of 1798 was an inquiry into the Variolae vaccinae , the pustules of the cow: his term for cowpox. People who had caught cowpox, usually from milking, turned out to be protected against smallpox. 1 The method spread and the name went with it. Vaccines are made in many ways now and almost none of them involve a cow, but the word still says where the first one was found. 1 2 The vaccine was given in two doses.

title: malaria
description: Malaria is the Italian mala aria, bad air. The disease was thought to rise off marshes as a vapour; the explanation went and the name stayed.
text: Malaria is a disease carried by mosquitoes. The name is the Italian mala aria , bad air. 1 It was named for what people believed caused it. Fevers were common around marshes, and the vapour coming off stagnant water was held to be what made people ill. 1 2 The parasite was identified in 1880 and the mosquito was shown to carry it before the century was out. The air had nothing to do with it. 2 The name did not change with the theory. We understand the disease now, and it is still called after an idea about air that nobody believes. 1 Malaria is still one of the world’s deadliest diseases.

title: school
description: School came through the Latin schola from the Greek skholē, which meant spare time, leisure, rest.
text: A school is a place people are taught in. The word came through the Latin schola from the Greek skholē , which meant spare time, leisure, rest. 1 2 The connection is less odd than it looks. Free time was what you needed in order to sit and argue about something, so the word moved from the time to the discussion held in it, and then to the people holding the discussion and the place they held it in. 1 2 Latin kept some of that width. Schola could mean leisure for learning, a lecture, a debate, or a place of learning. 1 2 English took the narrowest of those senses: a building, a register and a timetable. 1 She teaches at a school in the city.

title: magazine
description: Magazine comes from the Arabic makhzan, a storehouse. The ammunition store, the periodical and the part of a rifle are the same idea three times.
text: A magazine is something you read. The word comes from the Arabic makhzan , a storehouse or depot, and reached English through French in the 1580s. 1 Its first English sense was the literal one: a warehouse, and particularly a store of military supplies and ammunition. 1 In 1731 Edward Cave started a monthly in London called The Gentleman’s Magazine , made up of pieces gathered from other publications. He meant the word as it sounds, a storehouse of writing, and it is the first periodical the word was used for. 1 2 The rifle kept the older sense. The part that holds the cartridges is a magazine because it is where they are stored. The shelf at the newsagent and the box of ammunition are named for the same thing. 1 The article ran in a monthly magazine.

title: horde
description: Horde goes back to the Turkic ordu, a ruler’s camp and then any army. In English it came out meaning a disorderly crowd.
text: A horde is a large, disorderly crowd. The word goes back to the Turkic ordu , camp or army: the ruler’s encampment first, and then any military one. 1 2 It reached English in the 1550s by a long route, through Turkic into Russian and Polish and on westward. The h at the front appears to have been picked up in Polish. 1 It travelled with the Golden Horde and the armies of the steppe, seen from outside and at a distance. By the 1610s the word was being used for any uncivilised gang. 1 An ordu is an organised thing, with a chain of command and a place for everything. A horde is a rabble. The word travelled west and ended up meaning the opposite of what it started as. 1 2 A horde of tourists filled the square.

title: turquoise
description: Turquoise is the Old French for Turkish: pierre turqueise, the Turkish stone. It is named for the route it arrived by, not the ground it came out of.
text: Turquoise is a blue-green stone, and since the nineteenth century a colour as well. The name comes from the Old French turqueise , Turkish, in the phrase pierre turqueise : the Turkish stone. 1 The stone was not Turkish. The finest of it was mined in Persia, and Europe knew it because Venetian merchants bought it in Turkish markets and the overland routes ran through Ottoman territory. 1 2 So the name records the way it came rather than where it came from. The colour was named after the stone in the 1850s, and the colour is now what most people mean by the word: a country’s name, on a paint chart. 1 The ring was set with turquoise.

title: algebra
description: Algebra comes from al-jabr in the title of al-Khwarizmi’s ninth-century book: the restoring of something broken, a bone included.
text: Algebra comes from the Arabic al-jabr , out of the title of a book al-Khwarizmi wrote in Baghdad in the ninth century, Hisab al-jabr w’al-muqabala . 1 Al-jabr is restoring, or reuniting what is broken. In the book it names a particular move: a term subtracted on one side is restored by adding it to the other, until the equation balances. 1 2 The everyday sense travelled with the word. When algebra first came into English in the sixteenth century it could still mean the surgical setting of a fracture, and in Spanish an algebrista was a bone-setter. 3 The same book gave the other word. Algorithm came out of the author’s name. 1 He teaches algebra to first-year students.

title: lunatic
description: Lunatic comes from the Latin luna, moon, and the belief that madness followed the moon’s phases. It stayed in English law until 1930.
text: A lunatic is a madman, in the loose and old-fashioned way the word is used now. It comes from the Latin luna , moon, through the Late Latin lunaticus , moon-struck. 1 The idea behind it was a medical one: that some kinds of madness came and went with the phases of the moon, and that the moon was what moved them. 1 The belief went, and the word stayed in the law long after it. English statutes used lunatic as a legal category into the twentieth century, and it was the Mental Treatment Act of 1930 that turned lunatics, officially, into patients. 2 Nobody who uses the word now is thinking about the moon. Some lunatic overtook us on the bend.

title: pupil
description: The pupil of the eye is the Latin pupilla, little doll: the small figure of yourself you can see reflected in it.
text: The pupil of the eye is the dark opening in the middle of the iris. The word is the Latin pupilla , a little doll, a diminutive of pupa , girl or doll. 1 2 It is named after what you see in it. Stand close enough to someone and there is a tiny figure of you in their eye, about doll-sized. Greek did the same thing with korē , girl, which meant both the doll and the pupil. 1 The schoolchild comes from the same Latin root by another road. Pupillus and pupilla also meant an orphan or a minor in someone’s care, and the English pupil began as that legal sense before it meant anyone being taught. 1 2 The doctor checked his pupils.

title: salary
description: Salary comes from the Latin salarium, formed from sal, salt. The familiar claim that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is in no ancient source.
text: A salary is what you are paid for your work. It came through French from the Latin salarium , which is formed from sal , salt. That much is not in dispute. 1 The story attached to it is that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, and the story has a source. Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century, says salt is bound up with public honours and military service, and that salarium is named from it. 2 That is all he says. He does not write that soldiers were paid in salt, and no other ancient writer does either. The sentence about legions receiving salt instead of coin appears to be a later addition, filled in by dictionary-makers who wanted the connection to mean something definite. 3 So the salt is genuinely in the word and the reason for it is missing. I could not find an ancient source for the payment, and the scholarship says there is none to find. 2 3 She took a cut in salary.

title: assassin
description: Assassin comes from hashishi, a term of abuse used against the Nizari Ismailis. The hashish story that travelled to Europe with it is a legend.
text: An assassin kills someone prominent, usually for political reasons. The word came into European languages from variants of the Arabic hashishi , plural hashishiyya . 1 It was not a description. Other Muslims used it against the Nizari Ismailis as an insult, in the sense of low-class rabble or people of lax morals, with no claim attached that they used the drug. 1 The literal reading came later, and from outside. Crusader-era reports and then Marco Polo told of an Old Man of the Mountain who drugged young men and showed them a garden of paradise so they would kill on command. Farhad Daftary’s work on those accounts traces them to European invention and rumour rather than to anything recorded at Alamut. 1 2 The legend crossed into English and took the word with it. The drug is still in the name, and nobody has been able to show it was ever there. 1 2 He was killed by an assassin.

title: sabotage
description: Sabotage comes from sabot, a wooden shoe, but not from throwing one into a machine. The clog story is recorded nowhere.
text: Sabotage is damage done on purpose to stop something working. It is a French word, taken into English early in the twentieth century, from sabot , a wooden shoe or clog. 1 2 The story everybody knows is that workers threw their clogs into the machinery. It is repeated everywhere and recorded nowhere: no account of anyone actually doing it has been produced. 2 The likelier route is duller and stays inside the language. French saboter meant to clatter about in wooden shoes, and from there to work clumsily, and from there to botch a job on purpose. 1 2 The clog is in the word either way. Nobody can show that one was ever thrown into a machine. 2 The line was shut down by sabotage.

title: bank
description: Bank comes from the Italian banca, a bench: the counter a money-changer worked at. Bankrupt is built from the same table.
text: A bank is an institution that holds money. The word comes from the Italian banca , a bench, which was also used for the bench-like counter a money-changer worked at, and then for the shop itself. 1 2 The trade travelled from Italy to France and England and the word went with it. The marble hall and the application on a phone both started as a table in a market. 2 The bank refused the loan.

title: eavesdrop
description: The eavesdrop was the strip of ground where rain fell off a roof. Someone standing in it, against the wall, was an eavesdropper.
text: To eavesdrop is to listen to something you are not part of. The word was a place before it was an act. 1 The eavesdrop, or eavesdrip, was the strip of ground around a building where the rain came off the eaves. Old English had it as yfesdrype , and it mattered in law: you could not build too near your neighbour’s boundary, because your roof would drain onto their land. 1 2 Anyone standing in that strip is standing against the wall, under the eaves, close enough to hear what is said inside. By the fifteenth century that person had a name. The verb came later, out of the name. 1 2 He was eavesdropping on the next table.

title: farce
description: Farce comes from the Latin farcire, to stuff. It meant forcemeat first, then the comic matter stuffed in among the scenes of a religious play.
text: A farce is a comedy of slammed doors and mistaken identity. Said of anything else, it is a thing that has stopped being serious. It comes from the Latin farcire , to stuff or cram. English borrowed it first in the fourteenth century, and it meant forcemeat: the stuffing itself. 1 2 The theatre took the word from the kitchen. Phrases were stuffed into the fixed words of the liturgy at festivals, and the same word was then used for the comic business stuffed in among the scenes of a religious play. 1 2 The stuffing grew into a form of its own. English borrowed the word a second time in the sixteenth century, and that time it meant the comedy. 2 The trial was a farce.

title: idiot
description: Idiot comes from the Greek idiōtēs, a private person: someone who held no office and took no part in public affairs.
text: An idiot is a fool. The word comes from the Greek idiōtēs , from idios , one’s own, private. An idiōtēs was a private person: not in the public eye, holding no office. 1 2 It said nothing about intelligence. It described what a person did not take part in. From there the word went to the common man, and from the common man to the ignorant one, since ordinary people were not generally the ones with the learning. 1 2 English took it in that ignorant sense and then narrowed it again, from a man without education to a man without sense. 2 Some idiot had left the gate open.

title: inaugurate
description: Inaugurate comes from the Latin inaugurare, to consecrate by augury: to install someone once the omens had been read in the birds.
text: To inaugurate is to install someone in office, or to open something formally. The word comes from the Latin inaugurare , built on augur . 1 2 An augur was a Roman priest who read the will of the gods in birds: how they flew, how they fed, what they called. The job was to find out whether the gods approved of a thing being started at all. It was not a way of predicting what would happen. 1 2 So a man was inaugurated—installed once the birds had been consulted and the answer was yes. Nothing of consequence was begun without it. 2 Presidents are still inaugurated. The birds dropped out of the ceremony and stayed in the word. 1 The new building was inaugurated in May.

title: juggernaut
description: Juggernaut is an English rendering of Jagannath, whose temple cars at Puri are vast and hard to stop. The horror the word carries was supplied by missionary accounts.
text: A juggernaut is a force that flattens whatever is in front of it. The word is an English rendering of Jagannath, a deity of eastern India whose name means lord of the universe. 1 One part of the image is plain enough. At the Rath Yatra in Puri, enormous chariots carrying the deities are pulled through the streets by hundreds of people, and something that heavy is genuinely hard to stop or steer once it is moving. 1 The rest was supplied. Claudius Buchanan, an Anglican chaplain who had seen the festival, published Christian Researches in Asia in 1811; it became one of the most widely read English accounts of India of its day. He wrote the procession up as a scene of heathen horror, in support of the case for Christian missions, and that is the book the English word came through. 2 English kept the crushing and left the rest behind. 1 2 The company became a juggernaut.

title: lecture
description: Lecture comes from the Medieval Latin lectura, a reading. In the medieval university it was exactly that: the book read out to students who had no copy.
text: A lecture is a talk given in order to teach something. The word comes from the Medieval Latin lectura , a reading, from legere , to read. 1 2 It meant that literally. In the medieval university the teacher read out of the book and the students wrote it down, because there was one book, it was expensive, and they did not have it. 1 The sense of a discourse on a subject, rather than a reading out of a text, appears in the 1530s. Printing had been at work for two generations by then. 1 A lecture is now an exposition, and often anything but a reading. The word still names the older arrangement: a room with one copy of the book in it. 1 2 The lecture was at nine on Monday.

title: melancholy
description: Melancholy is the Greek melankholia, black bile. It names the fluid that was held to cause the mood, in a medicine nobody practises now.
text: Melancholy is a settled, quiet sadness. The word is the Greek melankholia , from melas , black, and kholē , bile. 1 2 It began as a diagnosis. In the medicine that ran from Hippocrates through Galen and on into the eighteenth century, the body held four humours—blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile—and the mixture of them made a person’s temperament. Too much black bile made you melancholy. 1 2 There is no black bile. The humours were abandoned and the treatments went with them, but the word outlived the physiology it was built on. 1 2 A melancholy that lasted all winter.

title: nostalgia
description: Nostalgia was coined in a medical dissertation of 1688, from the Greek nostos, homecoming, and algos, pain. It was the name of an illness.
text: Nostalgia is a fond feeling about the past. It started as the name of an illness. 1 2 Johannes Hofer, a medical student at Basel, made the word for his dissertation of 1688 out of the Greek nostos , homecoming, and algos , pain. It was his Latin for the German Heimweh , homesickness, and he described it as a disease of the brain. 1 2 The patients were often Swiss mercenaries serving abroad, set off by a remembered sight or a tune from home. They stopped eating and sleeping. It was taken seriously enough to be treated, and seriously enough to be written down as a cause of death. 3 The word softened as the illness stopped being one. The ache stayed. The algos is half the word. 1 2 A wave of nostalgia for the nineties.

title: rival
description: Rival comes from the Latin rivalis, from rivus, a stream: the people who drew water from the same watercourse.
text: A rival is someone competing with you for the same thing. The word comes from the Latin rivalis , from rivus , a stream. 1 2 Rivales were the people who took water from the same watercourse. It was a legal relationship before it was a hostile one: Roman law had provisions for what to do when two of them disagreed. 1 2 The water fell away as the word moved through French into English in the later sixteenth century. The competition stayed, mostly over love or honour rather than irrigation. 1 2 The shape of the old sense is still there. A rival is an opponent who draws on the same supply you do. 1 2 He was her closest rival.

title: trivia
description: Trivia is the Latin plural of trivium, the place where three roads meet. What was said at a crossroads was public, and then commonplace.
text: Trivia are small facts of no great weight. The word is the Latin plural of trivium , the place where three roads meet. 1 A crossroads is a public place. Anyone might be standing in it, and what was said there was what anyone might say, so trivialis came to mean public, and then ordinary, and then of no particular importance. 1 The medieval university used the same word for the first three of the seven liberal arts—grammar, rhetoric and logic—the ones taken before the other four. To be trivial was to belong to that first stage. 1 2 The sense the word has now, facts asked and answered for their own sake, is from the 1960s and American campuses. 1 He is unbeatable at trivia.

title: utopia
description: Thomas More built Utopia in 1516 out of the Greek for no place. The island where everything is right is named for not existing.
text: A utopia is an imagined society in which everything has been got right. Thomas More made the word up in 1516, as the name of the island in his book. 1 2 He built it from the Greek ou , not, and topos , place: no place. The joke is that it is a syllable away from eu-topos , good place, and More points at it himself—an addendum to the book has a verse saying the island ought rightly to be called Eutopia, the place of happiness. 1 2 Both readings sit in the word at once, and the book does not choose between them. 1 Their plan was a utopia and everybody knew it.

title: window
description: Window is the Old Norse vindauga, wind eye. It replaced Old English words that called the same hole an eye-hole and an eye-door.
text: A window is a hole in a wall with glass in it. The word is the Old Norse vindauga , from vindr , wind, and auga , eye: the wind’s eye. 1 2 It came into English in the early thirteenth century and named what there was then—an unglazed opening, often in a roof, that let in the weather along with the light. The wind is in the name because the wind came in. 1 Old English had its own words for it: eagþyrl , eye-hole, and eagduru , eye-door. Both were replaced, but everyone involved had seen the same thing in it—an eye in a wall. 1 She opened the window.

title: X-ray
description: Röntgen called the new rays X because nobody knew what they were. The X is the mathematician’s unknown, and it was never replaced.
text: An X-ray is radiation used to see inside things. Wilhelm Röntgen found it in November 1895, working with a covered cathode-ray tube, and announced it in a short paper called On a New Kind of Rays . 1 2 He called them X-rays. The X is the one from algebra, the letter you put where a quantity is not known yet. He did not know what the rays were and said so in the name. 1 2 German and several other languages call them Röntgen rays instead. He preferred his own placeholder, and English kept it. 1 2 The rays were explained long ago. The word still says nobody knows. 1 The X-ray showed a hairline fracture.

title: yacht
description: Yacht is the Dutch jacht, from jagen, to hunt or chase: a fast boat built to catch pirates, before it had anything to do with leisure.
text: A yacht is a boat for pleasure. The word is the Dutch jacht , shortened from jachtschip , hunting ship, from jagen , to hunt or chase. 1 2 It was built for the chase. Dutch warships were too heavy to catch the pirates and smugglers working their coast, so lighter and faster craft were made to run them down. 1 2 One was presented to Charles II in 1660, and he used it to go out on the water for the pleasure of it. English gentlemen wanted the same, and the word stopped meaning the chase. 1 2 They spent August on a yacht.

title: zero
description: Zero goes back to the Arabic sifr, empty. The same word entered Europe twice and came out as two English words: zero and cipher.
text: Zero is nothing, written down. The word goes back to the Arabic sifr , empty, which was itself used to render the Sanskrit śūnya , empty—the name Indian mathematicians gave the mark that held an empty place. 1 2 Europe took the word twice. One route latinised it as cifra , which gave English cipher ; the other, through Fibonacci’s zephirum , gave Italian zefiro and then zero . 1 2 3 So the two are the same word arriving by different roads. Cipher carried both senses into English: zero, in its older use, and a code. 3 The total came to zero.

title: bankruptcy
description: Bankruptcy is built on bankrupt, which came from the Italian banca rotta, a broken bench. Whether a bench was ever actually broken is another matter.
text: Bankruptcy is what happens when someone cannot pay what they owe. It is built on bankrupt , which came into English from the Italian banca rotta : a broken bench. 1 2 The bench is real. Banca was the ordinary Italian word for the table a money dealer worked at, and it is the same word that gave us bank . Rotta is broken, from the Latin rumpere . 2 The breaking is the story. A dealer who could not meet his debts had his table broken in front of him, and that was the end of his trade. Samuel Johnson retold it in his dictionary of 1755. 2 3 Nobody has produced evidence that it happened. The reading the dictionaries settle on is that rotta is figurative here, in the way an English business is said to be broken, and that no carpentry was involved. I could not confirm the custom. 1 2 Breaking the instrument of an office was a real way of ending one. A degraded knight had his belt cut, his spurs struck off and his sword broken over his head; a Garter knight’s banner was pulled down and thrown out of the chapel; and judges have snapped the nib of the pen that signed a death sentence, on the reasoning that it should not be used again. 4 5 Nothing I found joins any of that to the money dealer’s table. It does explain why the table is easy to picture: a reader who knows that a broken sword ends a knighthood will read a broken bench the same way. The company filed for bankruptcy.

title: serendipity
description: Horace Walpole coined serendipity in a letter of 1754, after a story whose princes found things they had not gone looking for.
text: Serendipity is the ability to find good things by accident. The word can also mean such a find itself. 1 In a letter dated January 28, 1754, Horace Walpole wrote about a painting. In the same letter he described a discovery he had made about a Venetian coat of arms while looking through an old book at random. He said this discovery was almost of the kind he called serendipity . 1 2 He took the word from the title of a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip . Serendip was an old name for Sri Lanka. As the princes traveled, they kept finding things they had not set out to find, by chance and by their own good sense. 1 2 Walpole’s word held both parts of the story: the accident, and the judgment to see what the accident had brought. 1 2 Finding that letter in the archive was pure serendipity.

title: mentor
description: Mentor was a character in the Odyssey. Athena took his form to guide Telemachus; a later French novel helped turn his name into a common noun.
text: A mentor is someone who guides a less experienced person. The word was a person’s name first. 1 In Homer’s Odyssey , Mentor was a trusted friend of Odysseus. When Athena went to help Odysseus’s son Telemachus, she appeared in Mentor’s form. The advice came from the goddess, though the young man saw his father’s friend. 1 2 Mentor took on a larger role in François Fénelon’s 1699 novel Les aventures de Télémaque . After that book, his name became a general word for a trusted guide in French and then in English. 2 Her first editor became her mentor.

title: quixotic
description: Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, the literary character whose pursuit of noble goals could take little account of the world around him.
text: A quixotic plan is driven by an ideal that may be impossible to carry out. The adjective comes from a character in a book. 1 Don Quixote, in Miguel de Cervantes’s novel, sets out to live as a knight. He sees a world of quests and enemies where other people see ordinary things. When he spots windmills on a plain, he takes them for giants. Sancho Panza tells him what they are, but Quixote charges them anyway. After he falls, he decides an enchanter must have turned the giants into windmills. 2 His name first became a word for a person like him, a Quixote , and then an adjective. Quixotic can admire someone’s commitment to a noble aim while questioning whether the aim can be reached. 1 The plan to restore every abandoned house was quixotic.

title: decimate
description: Decimate once meant selecting one soldier in ten for punishment. The Roman practice was far less routine than the word’s origin can make it sound.
text: To decimate a group is to kill or destroy a large part of it. The word holds a more exact number from an older use: ten. 1 The Latin decimare meant to punish every tenth person. Accounts of Roman military discipline describe soldiers chosen by lot, one in ten, from a disgraced unit and put to death. 1 2 That does not mean Roman commanders routinely killed a tenth of their men. The evidence for its use in the Republic is sparse, and a study of the practice argues that it was revived in the late Republic after long periods without it. 2 Today decimate usually means to devastate, even when the loss is much more than ten percent. The tenth remains in the word, though it is no longer a rule for using it. 1 The disease decimated the herd.

title: emoji
description: Emoji is Japanese for picture character. Early Japanese phone networks had their own sets before Unicode helped make them readable across devices.
text: An emoji is a picture character used in a message. Its name is Japanese: e means picture, and moji means character. The word has no etymological connection to the English emotion . 1 Emoji were used on Japanese mobile phones before they became familiar around the world. Different phone companies had their own sets and their own ways of encoding them. A symbol sent from one network could fail to appear as intended on another. 2 Unicode brought many of those characters into a common standard in 2010. A word from Japanese phones now names pictures that can travel between devices almost anywhere. 2 She ended the message with a laughing emoji.

title: muscle
description: Muscle comes from Latin musculus, little mouse. A flexing muscle may have suggested an animal moving under the skin.
text: A muscle contracts to move part of the body. Its name comes from the Latin musculus , a little mouse. 1 The likely image is a muscle moving under the skin when someone flexes, with its tendon suggesting a tail. The comparison is easy to test on an arm, though the reason for the name is given as probable rather than certain. 2 The muscle in his arm tightened.

title: lens
description: An optical lens was named for its resemblance to a lentil. The Latin lens meant the seed before it named the glass.
text: A lens bends light so that an image can be seen or made. The word first named something that could be eaten. 1 In Latin, lens meant a lentil. A lens that curves outward on both sides has much the same shape as the seed. That resemblance gave the piece of glass its name. 1 She changed the lens on her camera.

title: camera
description: Camera meant a room. In a camera obscura, light entering a dark chamber cast an image inside; the name later went to the device that recorded it.
text: A camera records an image. The word comes from the Latin for a room or chamber. 1 In a camera obscura , a darkened room or box, light enters through a small opening or lens. An image of the outside appears on the surface opposite. It can be viewed or traced onto paper. 2 Some versions were large enough to enter; others were boxes an artist could take outside. Later, photographic materials made it possible to preserve the image instead of drawing it by hand. 3 When photography developed, the shortened name went to the device that recorded the image. 3 4 He left his camera on the table.

title: climate
description: Climate goes back to a Greek word for inclination. It once marked zones by the angle of the sun before it named their long-term weather.
text: Climate now means the usual weather conditions of a place over a long time. The word began with an angle. 1 2 The Greek klima meant an inclination. Ancient geographers divided the earth into zones by latitude and the angle of the sun’s rays. Places at similar latitudes received the noon sun at a similar angle, and were placed in the same zone. 1 3 Weather came to define the word more fully. Rain, wind, altitude, and local geography also matter to a place’s climate. 3 The island has a mild climate.

title: museum
description: Museum comes from a Greek place of the Muses. In antiquity the name could belong to a place of learning and research, not only a collection of objects.
text: A museum keeps and studies objects and makes them available to visitors. Its name goes back to the Greek Mouseion , a place connected with the Muses. 1 2 In antiquity, such a place could be a shrine, a school or a place of study. The Museum at Alexandria housed scholars who worked there, with a common dining hall and places to walk and talk. 2 The city’s famous library was closely tied to it, though sources differ on whether it was part of the Museum or a separate institution. 2 3 The modern museum still studies what it holds. The definition the International Council of Museums adopted in 2022 names research, collecting and conservation alongside exhibition. 4 The museum has a collection of old maps.

title: gossip
description: Gossip once meant a godparent or close companion. Shakespeare’s plays preserve both the older sense and the later insult.
text: A gossip was once someone connected to a family through baptism. The Old English word godsibb joined God with kinship and referred to a godparent. Its meaning widened to include a close friend or companion. 1 2 Several meanings were still in use in Shakespeare’s time. In Henry VIII , the king addresses his daughter’s godparents as “My noble gossips.” In Titus Andronicus , Aaron calls the nurse “a long-tongued, babbling gossip.” One use belongs to a christening ceremony. The other expresses distrust of someone who might reveal a secret. 3 4 The word also became associated with women attending a birth and with the conversation at those gatherings. Its familiar sense developed alongside older meanings that remained available to speakers and writers. 2 He was a terrible gossip, though everyone told him things.

title: apron
description: Apron began as napron. Speakers divided a napron as an apron, while Scots and northern English dialects preserved the older initial n.
text: English once had napron , borrowed from French naperon , a word for a small cloth. In English it came to mean a covering worn over clothes to protect them. 1 Say “a napron” aloud. The same sounds can be divided as “an apron.” Over time, speakers attached the initial n to the article, and the shortened form became established. Edinburgh records from 1508 already contain the spelling apronis . 1 2 The older form survived elsewhere. The Dictionaries of the Scots Language records napron and related spellings with their initial n intact, and notes their use in northern English dialects too. The change spread unevenly, leaving different versions of the same word in use. 3 She wiped the flour from her hands onto her apron.

title: pamphlet
description: Pamphlet takes its name from a medieval Latin poem. The small booklets later carried political arguments and installments of novels.
text: The word comes from Pamphilus, seu de Amore , a popular Latin poem about love written in the twelfth century. Copies circulated as small booklets, and a form of the title gradually became a name for short works of this kind. Pamphilus was the central character’s name. 1 2 The word was already in use for handwritten works before printing reached England. Printed pamphlets later carried political arguments and news, often cheaply enough to reach readers who could afford few books. 2 The format also served fiction. Dickens’s David Copperfield appeared in monthly parts bound in paper wrappers. Those installments belong to the history of pamphlet binding too. A small folded publication could carry a public dispute or another portion of a novel whose readers were still waiting to learn what happened next. 3 Someone had left a pamphlet on every seat.

title: dunce
description: Dunce comes from the name of John Duns Scotus, a respected medieval thinker whose followers later became targets of academic ridicule.
text: To call someone a dunce is to call them slow to learn. The word comes from John Duns Scotus, a medieval philosopher admired for the subtlety of his thinking. 1 Scotus studied and taught at major European universities. His lectures on Peter Lombard’s Sentences , a central work of medieval theology, became a widely read commentary. Glasgow University Library holds a printed edition from 1477, nearly 170 years after his death. 2 His reputation changed as humanism gained ground in the sixteenth century. Followers who defended his teaching were ridiculed for resisting the new learning. Duns , a name associated with a school of thought, became a term of contempt. It acquired the spelling dunce and broadened into an insult for someone considered incapable of learning. 1 2 He felt like a dunce when he finally understood the instructions.

title: tulip
description: Tulip traces back through Turkish tülbent to Persian dulband, a turban. Early botanical texts compare the flower with a head covering.
text: The name of the tulip goes back through European languages to Turkish tülbent , borrowed from Persian dulband , meaning a turban. Tulip and turban are related words. 1 The Turkish name of the flower is lale . How a word for a head covering became its name elsewhere has attracted several explanations. One is that the flower was thought to resemble a turban. Another concerns the practice of wearing tulips on turbans and a supposed confusion between the flower and the thing beneath it. 2 The comparison with a head covering appears in sixteenth-century botanical writing. Johannes Kentmann’s notes link the flower’s shape with a Dalmatian cap. John Gerard later describes petals turning back as the flower opens, giving it the appearance of a Dalmatian or Turkish cap. 3 A 2022 study examined these early texts. Its authors found the comparison, but no sixteenth-century evidence for the familiar story of a translator mixing up the names. The connection with a turban is well established; the conversation sometimes offered to explain it remains unconfirmed. 1 3 The first tulip opened beside the garden wall.

title: biscuit
description: Biscuit originally meant bread baked twice to dry it for keeping. The word now names quite different foods in Britain and America.
text: The word biscuit once described how the food was made. Early French pain bescuit meant bread cooked twice. A second baking dried it out, helping it keep on a long journey. The phrase was shortened, and English borrowed the name. 1 Ship’s biscuits became a staple of life at sea. They could be so hard that biting into them was difficult, and stored supplies were vulnerable to insects. Royal Museums Greenwich shows a surviving biscuit with holes made by biscuit beetles. 2 Its collection also includes a biscuit made to an 1846 recipe. 3 The word eventually covered foods made without a second baking. In Britain, a biscuit is usually what Americans call a cookie. In the United States, it commonly means a small, soft quick bread. The old cooking instruction remains in the name of both. 1 She split a warm biscuit and spread it with butter.

title: silhouette
description: Silhouette comes from the name of a French finance minister. The inexpensive profile portraits could be made quickly and sent to distant friends.
text: A silhouette shows a figure by its outline, usually filled with a single dark color. The word comes from Étienne de Silhouette, who briefly served as France’s finance minister in 1759. 1 One explanation connects the name with his unpopular economies. Cheap or spare things were mockingly described as à la Silhouette , and the name became attached to inexpensive profile portraits. Other explanations refer to his short time in office, so the precise reason for the association remains uncertain. 1 2 A likeness of this kind could be cut from paper or painted quickly, cost relatively little, and travel easily in a letter. 2 Photography later offered another affordable way to keep a likeness, and silhouette portraits became less fashionable. 1 2 She recognized his silhouette at the window.

title: petrichor
description: Petrichor names the earthy smell associated with rain after dry weather. Two researchers formed the word from stone and the fluid of the Greek gods.
text: Petrichor is the earthy smell associated with rain after a dry spell. The word joins Greek petra , stone, with ichor , the fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods. 1 The name appeared in a 1964 paper by Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, researchers at Australia’s CSIRO. Their article, Nature of Argillaceous Odour , was published in Nature on March 7. 2 The smell was familiar long before it had a scientific name. Indian perfumers had already captured an earthy scent in sandalwood oil. By steam-distilling rocks that had been exposed to warm, dry conditions, Bear and Thomas obtained a yellowish oil associated with the odor, which moisture helped release. 1 Petrichor drifted through the open window when the rain began.

title: culture
description: Culture began with cultivation and care. Cicero used cultura animi for the cultivation of the mind, extending an image rooted in tending the land.
text: The Latin cultura meant cultivation or tending. It came from colere , a verb used for working the land and caring for things. The connection with agriculture was already a metaphor in Roman writing. Cicero used cultura animi , the cultivation of the mind. 1 English borrowed culture in the fifteenth century for the working of land. By about 1500, it could also describe the development of the mind through education. 2 In the nineteenth century it came to mean intellectual and artistic life, and the shared customs and achievements of a people. In a laboratory, microorganisms grown in a suitable environment are also called a culture . 2 Food is an important part of the region’s culture.

title: text
description: Text and textile share the Latin verb texere, to weave. Latin textus carried the image of woven material into the structure of a written work.
text: A text has a history of weaving. The Latin verb texere meant to weave or join things together. From it came textus , something woven, which was also used for the style or texture of a work. 1 The image passed into writing. Late Latin used textus for a written account, and medieval usage included the Scriptures and other written works. English acquired text through French in the late fourteenth century, when it could mean the wording of something written or an authoritative passage. 1 Textile comes from the same Latin verb, through textilis , meaning woven. The relationship between the two English words is easy to overlook because one belongs to writing and the other to fabric. Both retain the older idea of separate strands being joined into something continuous. 2 She read the text again and added a note in the margin.

title: sandwich
description: Sandwich takes its name from John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich. The familiar gambling story is uncertain; the word appears in Edward Gibbon’s journal in 1762.
text: On November 24, 1762, Edward Gibbon recorded an evening at a London club where men were eating sandwiches. His journal provides an early written record of the food’s English name, already familiar enough to use without explaining it. 1 The name is traced to John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich. The familiar account has him eating beef between slices of bread so that he could carry on gambling without leaving the table. It comes from the French travel writer Pierre-Jean Grosley, who visited London in 1765 and later described a minister spending twenty-four hours at a game with little else to eat. 2 That account is difficult to confirm. Grosley was passing on a story, and the evidence for Montagu as a compulsive gambler is weak. His biographer N. A. M. Rodger suggested that eating while working at his desk might explain the association instead. That remains a suggestion too. 2 Gibbon’s entry shows the name in use before Grosley’s visit. The meal that first attached the earl’s title to the food is harder to recover. 1 2 He packed a cheese sandwich for the journey.

title: cobalt
description: Cobalt takes its name from the German Kobold, a goblin blamed by miners when troublesome ores failed to yield the silver they expected.
text: The metal behind cobalt blue takes its name from a goblin. German miners used Kobold for a troublesome spirit, and the name became attached to ores that frustrated their attempts to extract useful metal. 1 In Saxony, miners tried smelting what they believed was silver-bearing ore. When it failed to yield the silver they expected, they blamed goblins for bewitching it. Some cobalt ores also contained arsenic, which could be released as poisonous fumes during processing. The material was dangerous as well as disappointing. 1 2 In the eighteenth century, the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt investigated a similar ore and identified a previously unrecognized metal. The miners’ name was carried over to the element. 2 Cobalt compounds give glass and ceramics a deep blue color. The name used for that familiar blue preserves the miners’ much less welcome experience of the ore. 1 The potter used cobalt to color the glaze.

title: wow
description: Wow appears in early Scots writing. In 1977, Jerry Ehman’s handwritten reaction to an unusual radio signal gave the Wow! signal its name.
text: Wow can sound very modern. The Dictionaries of the Scots Language records it in Peblis to the Play , with the example dated before 1500, and in Gavin Douglas’s writing of 1513. 1 Those early examples carry astonishment and fear as well as admiration. In one from 1540, someone cries out at what they see. In another, a frightened speaker asks for room to get away. 1 By 1924, American slang also used wow as a verb, for overwhelming someone with delight, the sense in which a performer wows an audience. 2 In 1977, the exclamation acquired a place in astronomy. On August 15, Ohio State University’s Big Ear radio telescope detected an unusually strong radio signal during a search for extraterrestrial intelligence. A few days later, the volunteer astronomer Jerry Ehman was reviewing the computer printout when he noticed the sequence 6EQUJ5 . He marked the characters in red and wrote “Wow!” in the margin. His colleague John Kraus began calling it the Wow! signal. 3 The six characters showed the signal growing stronger and then fading as the Earth’s rotation carried the telescope’s view past that part of the sky, which is what a compact radio source in the sky would do. 3 4 Follow-up observations have not detected the same signal again, and its origin remains unresolved. 3 4 Wow, I hadn’t realized how high we had climbed.

title: focus
description: Focus is the Latin word for a hearth. Kepler gave it to mathematics in 1604, probably after the point where a lens or a mirror gathers sunlight hot enough to start a fire.
text: A focus is a point where light rays meet, or a place at which we direct our attention. In Latin, focus meant a hearth. 1 2 Johannes Kepler gave the word to mathematics in 1604, in a book on the optical part of astronomy. He used it for the two points of an ellipse that are still called its foci. 3 The reason for a hearth is given as probable rather than certain. A lens or a curved mirror can gather sunlight onto one point and start a fire there. 1 2 From the point where rays meet, the word reached photography and ordinary speech. We can focus a camera, and we can focus our minds. 1 2 She adjusted the focus until the lettering was clear.

title: anatomy
description: Anatomy is Greek for a cutting up. The same root is in atom, what cannot be cut, and anatomy misheard once gave English atomy, a skeleton.
text: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body. The Greek anatomē , from which it comes, meant dissection, literally a cutting up. 1 The same Greek root for cutting is in atom . Greek atomos meant indivisible, that which cannot be cut. Anatomy names the cutting of a body into its parts; an atom was named as something that could not be cut at all. 1 2 In older English, an anatomy was also heard as an atomy , and atomy became a word of its own for a skeleton, or for a person thin enough to look like one. 3 Anatomy can now mean the body’s structure itself, and it can be used for the detailed examination of other things. 1 The students studied the anatomy of the hand.

title: placebo
description: Placebo means I shall please in Latin. It named a prayer service, then flattery, before becoming a term in medicine.
text: A placebo can be an inactive preparation given in a medical study. The word once belonged to a prayer. 1 In Latin, placebo means I shall please. It began a verse sung in the evening service for the dead, and the service came to be called by that first word. 1 2 In medieval English, to sing placebo could mean to flatter someone. By the eighteenth century, physicians used the word for something given to please a patient rather than for a specific therapeutic action. 1 2 Placebos later became important in controlled studies, where they help researchers distinguish the effects of a treatment from effects associated with receiving care and expecting improvement. A word from the service for the dead became part of the language of testing medicine. 1 Half the volunteers received a placebo.

title: parliament
