description: Parliament grew from an Old French word for speaking and discussion. The institution kept the name as assemblies changed.
text: A parliament is an assembly that debates and makes laws. Before it named an institution, the word named a conversation. 1 Old French parlement meant a speaking or discussion, from parler , to speak. English borrowed the word for formal gatherings in the Middle Ages. It came to mean an assembly summoned by a ruler. 1 2 The English Parliament grew out of the great councils at which the king met the leading men of the kingdom. Knights from the counties had sometimes been summoned before, and in 1265 the towns were also asked to send burgesses. It gradually became established that people outside the aristocracy would be summoned. 2 Parliament met again after the recess.

title: ballot
description: Ballot comes from an Italian word for a small ball used in voting. The name survived when votes were recorded on paper.
text: A ballot is a vote, or the paper on which someone records one. The word once referred to a small ball. 1 2 Italian ballotta meant a little ball. In Venice, small balls could be used to register votes without a public show of hands. English borrowed the word for this way of voting. 1 2 Paper ballots eventually took the place of the little balls, and the name went with them. The object changed, while the word kept its place in an election. 1 The voters marked their ballots in private.

title: meander
description: Meander is the name of a river in western Türkiye, the Maeander, now the Büyük Menderes. Its course was so winding that its name came to mean any winding course.
text: To meander is to wind slowly, as a river does, or a person with nowhere in particular to be. The word is the name of a river: Greek Maiandros , Latin Maeander . 1 The river still runs. It is the Büyük Menderes , the longest river in western Türkiye, which once divided the ancient regions of Caria and Lydia. 2 It was known for its bends. Strabo, writing about two thousand years ago, said its course was so winding that everything winding was called after it. 3 Greeks already used the river’s name for winding patterns. 1 English took the noun in the 1570s, first for an intricate confusion and from the 1590s for the bends of a river. The verb followed in the 1610s for a river’s winding flow, and by the 1830s a person could meander too. 1 We meandered along the shore with no plan.

title: clue
description: A clue was a ball of thread. The thread Ariadne gave Theseus, which led him out of the Labyrinth, turned the word into anything that shows the way.
text: A clue is something that helps you find an answer. It was once a clew , a ball of thread or yarn, from the Old English cliewen , a ball or skein. 1 The change came from a Greek myth. Ariadne gave Theseus a thread to take into the Labyrinth, and once he had killed the Minotaur he followed it back out. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses . 2 From the 1590s English used the word for anything that guides a person through an intricate case, and by the 1620s for whatever points the way, with no labyrinth involved. 1 The spelling changed as well. Middle English often wrote French words ending in -ue with -ew , and when their spelling went back to -ue , some native words followed, among them hue , true and clue . The spelling clue appears in the middle of the fifteenth century, and clew survived for the thread in northern English and Scots. 1 There was no clue to who had written the letter.

title: calculate
description: Calculate comes from the Latin calculus, a small pebble used as a counter. The stone is still there in a doctor’s calculus and in calcium.
text: To calculate is to work something out with numbers. The Latin calculare meant to reckon, and it was built on calculus , a small pebble, from calx , limestone. 1 The pebbles were counters. On a Roman counting board they were moved along grooves to hold the figures of a sum. 1 2 English took calculate in the 1560s. A century later calculus became the name of a method in mathematics. 1 Medicine kept the stone. Since the early eighteenth century a calculus has been a stone formed in the body, such as a kidney stone, and dentists use the word for hardened plaque. 1 The limestone kept its name too. When Humphry Davy isolated a new metal in 1808, he called it calcium, after calx . 3 She calculated how long the journey would take.

title: thrill
description: A thrill once pierced. The Old English þyrlian, to pierce, came from þyrel, a hole, the same hole that is still in nostril.
text: A thrill is a sudden rush of excitement or fear that seems to go right through you. The word began with exactly that. The Old English verb þyrlian meant to pierce, and it came from þyrel , a hole. In Middle English thirlen became thrillen , as two of its sounds changed places. 1 By the late fourteenth century the verb could be used of a feeling that pierces someone. The shivering, exciting feeling is recorded from the 1590s, and the noun from the 1670s. 1 The same hole is still in nostril . Old English nosþyrl was the hole of the nose, from nosu , nose, and þyrel . 2 A thrill went through the crowd when the doors opened.

title: divan
description: Divan began as a Persian word for written sheets. It became an office, a council, the seat along the council chamber’s walls and a poet’s collected poems.
text: A divan is a low sofa, usually without a back. The word began in Persian, where devan meant a bundle of written sheets or a small book. 1 In Arabic, dīwān moved from a book of accounts to the office that kept them, and from there to a government office and the council that met in its chamber. 1 2 English first took the word from Turkish in the 1580s, for a council of state. 1 The seat came from the room. The long cushioned benches along the walls of a council chamber were called divans, and English has used the word for a sofa since 1702. 1 Two other senses went their own way. A divan is also a poet’s collected poems, as in the Divan of Hafez. 1 2 In Italy the Arabic word became dogana , earlier doana , the customs house. 3 He fell asleep on the divan with the book still open.

title: saturnine
description: Saturnine means gloomy because astrology held that people born under Saturn shared its coldness and slowness. Saturn was also the alchemists’ name for lead.
text: A saturnine person is gloomy and slow to warm. The word means “of Saturn,” and in the fifteenth century it described someone born under that planet’s influence. 1 2 Saturn was thought to be the planet farthest from the Sun, and so the coldest and the slowest. Old medicine held that people born under it took on its nature. 1 Renaissance writers gave the planet a second side. Marsilio Ficino, himself born under Saturn, tied it to melancholy and to the deep thought of scholars, so that a child of Saturn could be gloomy and gifted at once. 3 Saturn was also the alchemists’ name for lead, so saturnine can mean “of lead.” Medicine still uses it that way: saturnine gout is caused by lead poisoning. 1 2 He gave a saturnine smile and said nothing.

title: jovial
description: Jovial means of Jove, another name for Jupiter. Astrology held that people born under the planet Jupiter were cheerful, and the word kept the cheer.
text: A jovial person is cheerful and good company. The word means “of Jove,” another name for Jupiter, the chief Roman god. It reached English from French in the 1580s with an astrological sense: under the influence of the planet Jupiter. 1 Astrology held that people shared the nature of the planet that ruled their birth. Those born under Jupiter were thought to be cheerful, and the word kept the cheer after the belief had gone. 1 2 It was often set against saturnine , gloomy. In Roman myth Saturn was Jupiter’s father. 2 Our jovial host kept everyone’s glass full.

title: mercurial
description: Mercurial first meant of the planet Mercury. Astrology gave those born under it the messenger god’s quickness, and the liquid metal probably helped the word mean changeable.
text: A mercurial person changes mood quickly and without warning. In the late fourteenth century the word meant “of the planet Mercury,” from Latin Mercurialis . 1 2 Mercury was also the Roman messenger god, quick and clever, and astrology gave his qualities to those born under his planet. By the 1640s English used mercurial for a lively, quick and changeable temperament. 1 The metal probably helped. Mercury, or quicksilver, stays liquid and runs at a touch, and medicine still calls anything containing it mercurial. 1 2 His mercurial temper kept everyone guessing.

title: bergamot
description: Bergamot first named a pear, traced to the Turkish bey armudu, the bey’s pear. Dictionaries disagree whether the citrus took that name or the name of the Italian town of Bergamo.
text: Bergamot is a small citrus fruit with a fragrant, bitter oil in its rind. 1 Where its name comes from is not settled. The word first named a pear. In the 1610s English used bergamot for an especially fine pear, and the Online Etymology Dictionary traces that name to the Turkish bey armudu , the bey’s pear, reshaped in Italian to sound like the town of Bergamo. 2 For the citrus, which came into English in the 1690s, the same dictionary takes the town itself: Bergamo, in northern Italy. 2 Merriam-Webster gives the citrus the Turkish pear instead. 1 Both dictionaries find the Turkish pear in the word. They disagree about whether the citrus owes its name to the pear or to the town. The tea smelled of bergamot.

title: hazard
description: Hazard was first a game of dice. It may go back to an Arabic word for a die, though that origin is doubted, and in English it came to mean a risk of harm.
text: A hazard is a danger, a risk that something will go wrong. In English it was first the name of a game of dice, around 1300. The French hasard meant the game and also a throw of six. 1 2 The word may have come into French from Arabic. Merriam-Webster traces it through Spanish azar to Arabic az-zahr , the die, probably borrowed during the Crusades. 2 That origin is doubted. The Online Etymology Dictionary notes that zahr does not appear in the classical Arabic dictionaries, and records Ernest Klein’s suggestion of yasara , he played at dice, instead. 1 The meaning moved from the throw to the chances of life. Since the 1540s a hazard in English has been a risk of loss or harm. 1 The ice on the steps is a hazard.

title: tragedy
description: Tragedy is the Greek tragōidia, a goat song. Why a goat is not known. The word went from a kind of play to any calamity.
text: A tragedy is a terrible event, and before that it was a kind of play with a sorrowful end. The Greek tragōidia is made of tragos , a goat, and ōidē , a song. 1 Why a goat is not known. One explanation looks to satyr plays, whose performers wore goatskins. Another looks to a singer who competed for a goat as a prize. Some doubt the goat altogether. 1 Aristotle wrote that tragedy began with the authors of the dithyramb and grew away from the grotesque manner of the satyric form. 2 English took the word in the late fourteenth century for a serious story that ends in misery. Chaucer, translating Boethius, defined it as prosperity that ends in wretchedness. By about 1500 a tragedy could be any calamity. 1 The fire was a tragedy for the whole street.

title: chauvinism
description: Chauvinism is named after Nicolas Chauvin, a soldier devoted to Napoleon who is known from an 1831 play. Whether a real Chauvin stood behind him has never been settled.
text: Chauvinism is a blind belief that one’s own group is better than others. The word is French, chauvinisme , and it is named after Nicolas Chauvin, a soldier who stayed devoted to Napoleon long after the Empire had ended. 1 2 Chauvin is known as a character. He appears in La Cocarde tricolore , a popular comic play by the brothers Théodore and Hippolyte Cogniard, staged in 1831. 1 2 Whether a real Chauvin stood behind him has never been settled. The name was common in Napoleon’s army, and an 1822 memoir mentions a Chauvin who came back with Napoleon from Elba, but no one has shown that he was the man. 1 English took chauvinism in 1840 for excessive patriotism. Male chauvinist was in use by 1936 and became common after 1969. 1 The speech was full of national chauvinism.

title: checkmate
description: Checkmate comes through French and Arabic from the Persian shāh, king. The same king gave English check, the Exchequer and, probably by way of it, the spelling cheque.
text: Checkmate ends a game of chess: the king is attacked and cannot escape. The word came into English in the fourteenth century from Old French eschec mat , from Arabic shāh māt . 1 The Arabic is usually read as “the king died.” But shāh is the Persian word for king, and Persian māt can mean astonished, so the phrase may first have meant that the king was left helpless rather than dead. 1 Check comes from the same shāh , and it travelled far from the board. The officials of the Norman kings of England counted the royal revenue with counters on a table covered with a chequered cloth, which looked like a chessboard, and their department became the Exchequer. 2 The bank cheque , from 1798, probably took its spelling from the exchequer. 1 Three moves later it was checkmate.

title: sherbet
description: Sherbet is the Turkish şerbet, a drink, from an Arabic word for a draught. Syrup came from the same Arabic root by an older road, and sorbet by a later one.
text: Sherbet is now a frozen dessert or, in Britain, a fizzy sweet powder. The word is the Turkish şerbet , a drink, from Persian sharbat and Arabic sharba , from the verb shariba , to drink. 1 In Arabic, sharba was a single draught, the amount drunk at one time. 2 English met the drink in the 1580s and spelled it many ways, among them sorbet , zerbet and cherbet . 1 The same Arabic root had reached English long before, by another road. Syrup came in the late fourteenth century through Old French sirop , from Arabic sharāb , a drink or wine. 1 The frozen sense arrived through Italian sorbetto in the eighteenth century, and in the nineteenth English took the French sorbet for it again. 1 They drank cold sherbet in the shade.

title: nice
description: Nice once meant foolish or ignorant. Its later meanings included fussy, delicate and precise before it became an everyday word of approval.
text: Calling someone nice is usually a compliment. When the word reached English from French in the late thirteenth century, it could mean foolish or ignorant. Behind it was Latin nescius , meaning unaware or not knowing. 1 The change took centuries. Among its later meanings were fussy and hard to please, then delicate and precise. Something nice could require careful attention or a discriminating taste. By the eighteenth century the word was also being used for things that pleased, and later for people who were kind or considerate. 1 Some of those meanings still coexist. A nice distinction is a subtle or precise distinction; someone with a nice palate is particular about what they taste. These uses preserve the exacting sense alongside the much broader approval in a nice day . 2 It was nice of her to wait for us.

title: silly
description: Silly descends from an Old English word for happiness and good fortune. Its history passes through innocence and helplessness on the way to foolishness.
text: Silly began with good fortune. Its Old English ancestor meant happy or fortunate, and the related German word selig still means blessed or blissful. In Middle English, forms such as sely and seely carried meanings including blessed and innocent. 1 2 Innocence could also suggest being harmless or unable to defend oneself. The word came to describe someone deserving pity, then someone weak. By the sixteenth century it could describe a person judged to lack sense. These meanings developed along overlapping paths, with innocence and helplessness giving way to foolishness. 1 Today silly can be a mild criticism of someone’s judgement or an affectionate word for playful behaviour. The older meanings survive in texts where a “silly” person may be helpless or humble. 2 I made a silly mistake when I copied the address.

title: awful
description: Awful once described something that inspired awe, fear or reverence. The same word now serves for an unpleasant meal or a bad day.
text: Awful carries awe inside it. In its older uses, something awful inspired fear or reverence. The word could describe the power of something that made people feel small or deeply respectful. 1 That strength gradually weakened in everyday use. By around the beginning of the nineteenth century, awful was being used for things that were very bad or disagreeable. It also became an intensifier: an awful lot is a great quantity. A word suited to dread could now describe a disappointing meal. 1 2 The older meaning remains available, especially in literary writing. Merriam-Webster gives George Eliot’s phrase “awful loveliness” as an example. There the beauty inspires awe. Reading it as a complaint would change the sense of the passage. 2 The weather was awful, so we stayed inside.

title: villain
description: Villain comes from a word for a villager or farm worker. Contempt for someone’s social rank became a judgement about their character.
text: The villain in a story has a name that once belonged to a villager. The word comes through French from Medieval Latin villanus , a rural inhabitant or farm worker, derived from villa . 1 2 In medieval usage, the name carried the contempt of people who ranked themselves above those who worked the land. A person of low birth was assumed to have coarse manners. The judgement then extended to morals: someone considered uncouth became someone considered wicked. 1 By the sixteenth century villain could mean a scoundrel. The familiar use for a character whose evil actions drive a play or novel came later. The spelling villein kept the historical sense of a peasant bound to a lord’s land, while villain became the usual form of the insult. 2 The villain was the most interesting character in the play.

title: prestige
description: Prestige once meant a trick or illusion. In the nineteenth century it developed the favourable sense of reputation and standing.
text: Prestige is the standing someone has in other people’s eyes. When English borrowed the word from French in the seventeenth century, it meant a trick or illusion. Its Latin ancestry belongs to conjuring and deception. 1 2 In the nineteenth century the word began to describe the impressive appearance of someone’s importance or ability. It could still suggest a flattering illusion, but it also came to mean the reputation itself. Admiration became part of the word’s ordinary meaning. 1 Prestigious had entered English separately, from a related Latin word meaning deceitful or full of tricks. It kept that sense for centuries before acquiring its familiar meaning of highly regarded around the beginning of the twentieth century. Both words had moved from deception to esteem. 2 The discovery brought considerable prestige to the university.

title: freelance
description: Freelance began as a name for a hired medieval warrior in nineteenth-century writing. The lance belonged to someone who could choose whom to serve.
text: A freelance worker takes on work without a lasting commitment to one employer. The word first named a hired warrior. The lance was a weapon, and its bearer could offer his service to whoever would pay. 1 The word appeared in the early nineteenth century. Merriam-Webster’s earliest written evidence comes from Walter Scott’s Ivanhoe , where a lord speaks of his “Free Lances” after offering their services to Richard. Scott was writing about medieval life long after the period itself. 1 The expression widened to include politicians who belonged to no party and people who worked independently. By the late nineteenth century it was being applied to journalism. The modern adjective keeps the idea of offering a skill without committing to a single employer. 1 2 She works as a freelance editor.

title: The black hole
description: Explore the light around a black hole in a watercolor picture, one detail at a time.
text: Accretion disk The gas gives us something to see. The bright band is gas moving around the black hole. Matter collects in a thin disk and gradually travels inward. This inward movement is accretion. The hot gas emits the light that makes the surroundings visible. Gas like this gave away the first system that astronomers widely believed to hold a black hole. Cygnus X-1 was found as a source of X-rays in 1964. In 1972, two separate studies showed that its bright star circles an unseen, massive companion. Its mass is now put at about 20 times the Sun’s. A black hole can also be alone, with little material nearby to feed such a disk. This picture shows one with gas around it, giving us a view we would lose if the gas were gone. Gravitational lensing The far side comes into view. The gas belongs to a flat disk. Light from its far side follows the curved paths of space-time near the black hole and reaches us above the dark center. The disk appears to rise into an arch. Gravity’s bending of light was first measured during the total solar eclipse of 29 May 1919. Two expeditions organized by Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the darkened Sun and found them shifted by a little under two arcseconds, in line with Einstein’s prediction. Near a black hole the same bending is strong enough to lift the far side of the disk into view. Look below the foreground band too. Another path brings light from the underside of the far side into view there. Our viewing angle changes these shapes. Looking straight down on the disk would give a very different picture. Black hole shadow The dark center is a shadow. Light that passes through the event horizon cannot reach us again. Gravity also bends nearby paths of light. Together, these effects create the dark region called the black hole’s shadow. The horizon first appeared on paper. Within two months of Einstein publishing his field equations in 1915, Karl Schwarzschild, an artillery lieutenant on the Russian front, found an exact solution for the space around a single mass. It contains a radius, now named after him, from inside which nothing can escape. He died soon afterward, still in military service. The shadow looks larger than the event horizon within it. The dark shape in this painting marks the shadow; its edge does not give us a view of the horizon itself. Photon ring Light that took a longer way. The fine rim around the shadow represents a photon ring. It contains highly distorted images of the disk, made by light that traveled around the black hole more than once before escaping toward us. In the model there are multiple rings, becoming thinner and fainter closer to the shadow. The painting simplifies them into a narrow line. The broad arch farther out is another image of the disk, with a different path to our eyes. Doppler beaming Motion changes the light we receive. The left side is brighter in this view because the gas there is moving toward us. Close to the black hole, its orbital speed is high enough for relativity to change the brightness of the light we receive. The receding side appears dimmer. This effect is called Doppler beaming. The contrast depends on our angle to the moving gas. Viewed from directly above the disk, that difference between approaching and receding sides would disappear. The 2019 image of the black hole in the galaxy M87 shows the same effect. Its ring is brighter on one side, and the Event Horizon Telescope team traced the difference to gas on that side moving toward us. In 1978, Jean-Pierre Luminet calculated how a black hole surrounded by a thin gas disk would look. He used an IBM 7040 computer at the Paris-Meudon Observatory, feeding it punched cards. To turn the numbers into an image, he placed ink dots on negative image paper, more densely where his calculation predicted more light, then reversed the image. The image first appeared in November 1978 in La Recherche, a French popular science magazine, and then in a technical journal in 1979. It already showed the distorted disk and unequal brightness that make this shape recognizable. Our watercolor is a new interpretation, separate from Luminet’s original image. On 10 April 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released the first image of a black hole’s shadow, at the center of the galaxy M87. Eight radio telescopes had collected the measurements in 2017; their combined data were used to reconstruct the image. A bright, uneven ring surrounded a dark center, broadly agreeing with the features predicted by earlier models. It was an observed image made from radio light. The painted disk above shows a different viewing angle, using an illustration to make individual paths of light easier to explore. The interior raises a question of its own. In the simple, non-rotating model pictured here, general relativity predicts a central singularity, where matter reaches infinite density. Astronomers do not know whether this describes something physical or marks a limit of the mathematics. Quantum effects may become essential there. The dark center in the painting represents the shadow seen from outside; it does not show the singularity. A white hole reverses the classical black-hole idea: matter and light can leave it, while nothing can enter. Stephen Hawking discussed white holes in his 1976 paper on black-hole thermodynamics, examining their relationship to black holes through time reversal. This was a theoretical argument. No white hole has been confirmed by observation, and a possible connection to a black hole remains speculative. Quasars once entered this speculation too. Some scientists considered whether their extraordinary brightness might come from white holes. Observations instead support a different explanation. A quasar is the intensely luminous active center of a galaxy, powered by gas falling toward a supermassive black hole. The light comes from material around the hole, before it crosses the event horizon. The black hole and the quasar name different parts of that system.

title: The quasar
description: Explore a quasar’s disk, particle jets and dusty surroundings in a watercolor reconstruction.
text: Accretion disk Falling gas powers the light. Gas gathers into a disk as it circles a supermassive black hole. Its inward movement releases gravitational energy and heats the gas. The disk becomes so luminous that a small region at the center of a galaxy can outshine the galaxy’s stars. This helps explain the early puzzle of quasars. A telescope could record a point of light that looked like a star, while the object’s distance implied an extraordinary energy output. The small bright disk in this reconstruction marks the source of much of that energy. Supermassive black hole The black hole sits inside the light. A quasar’s central black hole can contain millions or billions of times the Sun’s mass. Material around it gives off the light we receive before crossing the event horizon. Once light passes inside that boundary, it cannot escape to an outside observer. The dark mark here indicates the black hole’s location. Its size has been adjusted for the illustration. It is not an observed shadow, and it gives us no view of the interior. Particles and magnetic fields Some of the material flows outward. Some quasars launch narrow streams of particles from the region around their black holes. Strong magnetic fields help organize these jets, which can travel close to the speed of light. Their launch region lies outside the event horizon. The particles have not escaped from inside the hole. Jets from supermassive black holes can extend hundreds of thousands of light-years. This painting shows only a short stretch. Many quasars have no powerful jets; how the flow of gas, magnetic fields and black-hole spin produce one remains an active subject of research. Doppler beaming The other direction can be harder to see. The same system can send material in opposite directions and still appear strongly one-sided. When a jet points partly toward us and moves very fast, relativity increases the brightness we receive. The jet traveling away appears dimmer. Jets like these once seemed to outrun light. In 1970 and 1971, radio astronomers compared observations of the quasar 3C 279 made a few months apart and found two bright parts separating at about ten times the speed of light. The explanation that held is material moving close to the speed of light, partly toward us, which makes it appear to travel faster and makes the approaching side brighter. Martin Rees had predicted the effect in 1966. This effect on brightness is Doppler beaming. The unequal brightness in the watercolor represents it. A faint counterjet does not by itself mean the black hole is sending less material that way. Gas, dust and viewing angle Dust can hide the bright center. Farther from the hot inner disk, dust can survive. A thick, uneven ring of dusty gas surrounds the engine in this reconstruction. Depending on our viewing angle, it can obscure the bright center and change the kind of active galaxy we appear to see. ESO’s infrared observations of Messier 77 traced heated dust around a hidden central engine. Observations of another active galaxy, NGC 3783, also found substantial dust above and below the expected ring. The torus is a useful model; real dust distributions can be more complicated than a neat doughnut. In the early 1960s, the radio source 3C 273 had a visible counterpart that looked like a star, with a faint jet beside it. Its spectrum was puzzling. In 1963, Maarten Schmidt recognized familiar hydrogen lines at wavelengths much longer than expected. The lines had been shifted toward the red. Interpreting that shift through the expansion of the universe placed the object far beyond our galaxy. Distance changed what that point of light meant. The light from 3C 273 has taken roughly 2.5 billion years to reach us. To appear so bright from so far away, its source had to be exceptionally luminous. The name quasar preserves the early impression, shortened from “quasi-stellar radio source.” Astronomers came to understand these objects as intensely bright galactic centers powered by gas falling toward supermassive black holes. Some of that gas produces the disk and jets reconstructed above. The surrounding galaxy was difficult to see through the central glare. Hubble helped reveal the galaxies that quasars inhabit. In observations reported in 2024, astronomers used Hubble’s coronagraph to block the bright center of 3C 273 and examine its surroundings more closely. Structures near the core became visible, along with its long jet. The black circle in those telescope images belongs to the instrument’s mask. The painting brings parts of the system together at sizes that make them readable. Observations show the galactic surroundings and jets, while scientific models help reconstruct the much smaller central engine. The bright disk sits deep inside a far larger galaxy. The jet continues beyond this sheet, and the tiny dark mark at its origin represents a black hole inferred from what happens around it.

title: The visible surface
description: Its light is crossed by dark lines.
text: Most of the visible light we receive from the Sun comes from its photosphere. This is a layer of gas, with no solid ground beneath the bright face we see. Near the disk’s edge, our line of sight passes obliquely through that layer. We see cooler, dimmer material higher up, making the limb appear darker than the center. The fall in temperature with height also leaves dark lines in sunlight. In 1814 Joseph von Fraunhofer, who headed a glassworks at Benediktbeuern, found hundreds of them while testing the quality of his lenses. Each line belongs to a particular kind of atom absorbing light in the cooler gas above, and the lines later showed what the Sun is made of.

title: Sunspots
description: Magnetic fields keep the spots cooler.
text: The dark centers are called umbrae. Lighter, streaked penumbrae surround them. A sunspot still glows intensely and looks dark beside the hotter photosphere around it. In 1908 George Ellery Hale, at the Mount Wilson Solar Observatory, found that some lines in the light of sunspots were split in two, as lines split in the laboratory beside a strong magnet. It showed that sunspots hold strong, concentrated magnetic fields. The fields restrict the flow of heat toward the surface, so the spots are cooler than their surroundings. The number of spots rises and falls over a cycle of about 11 years. The pattern was found by Heinrich Schwabe, a pharmacist in Dessau, who watched the Sun on almost every clear day from 1825 while looking for a planet closer to it than Mercury. He reported it in 1843.

title: Prominence
description: A new element was found in its light.
text: A prominence is relatively cool, dense plasma held in the hot corona by magnetic fields. Its shape follows the field that supports it. In 1868 Pierre Janssen traveled to India to study a total eclipse and saw a new yellow line in the Sun’s spectrum. Later that year he and Norman Lockyer each found a way to observe prominences without an eclipse, and Lockyer recorded the same line in a prominence’s light, a little to one side of the yellow lines of sodium. The line pointed to a new element. It was named helium, from helios, the Greek word for the Sun, and was found on Earth in 1895. Against the dark sky beyond the limb, this material appears bright. Seen against the solar disk, a similar structure can appear as a dark filament. Prominences may persist for days or longer, and some erupt. The separate SDO image above records an erupting prominence on September 23, 2012, in extreme ultraviolet light. Its display color is assigned.

title: The corona
description: It can now be seen without an eclipse.
text: The corona is the Sun’s outer atmosphere. During a total solar eclipse, the Moon hides the much brighter photosphere and this outer atmosphere becomes visible around it. The separate SDO image above instead records extreme ultraviolet light at 171 angstroms, displayed in assigned color. Until 1931 the corona could be photographed only during an eclipse. Bernard Lyot designed an instrument that blocks the glare of the bright disk, the coronagraph, and on July 12, 1931, at the Pic du Midi Observatory, it gave the first photograph of the corona taken outside an eclipse. His studies of the corona’s faint spectral lines helped show that its gas is much hotter than had been thought. The corona can reach temperatures of a million degrees Celsius or more, far above the photosphere. Explaining how energy heats it remains an active area of research. Its streamers and loops change with the Sun’s magnetic activity, and some coronal material escapes into space as the solar wind.

title: What the light told us
description: What the light told us
text: The spots in this picture would move if we watched the Sun over successive days. Following sunspots across the disk gave astronomers a way to detect the Sun’s rotation. The movement also reveals that different parts turn at different rates. The equatorial region goes around faster than the poles. That is possible because the Sun is made of gas and plasma, with no rigid surface holding it to one pace. Light also carries evidence of what a star contains. In her 1925 doctoral thesis, Cecilia Payne used stellar spectra and the physics of ionization to study the abundance of elements. Her results pointed to enormous quantities of hydrogen and helium. That challenged the prevailing idea that stars had a composition much like Earth’s. The astronomer Henry Norris Russell urged caution, and Payne qualified the conclusion in her thesis. Four years later, Russell’s own work supported it. The bright disk above is the visible layer of a star made mostly of those two elements. The source of the light lies much deeper than the layer we can see. In the core, at about 15 million degrees Celsius, nuclear reactions fuse hydrogen into helium and release energy. Energy moves outward through the radiative zone and then the convection zone before reaching the photosphere. The visible surface shown here is about 5,500 degrees Celsius. It is the place from which much of the visible light escapes, far above the core that powers it. The faint corona brought another surprise. Its spectrum contained bright lines that did not match known materials, so astronomers proposed an element called coronium. The explanation turned out to be extreme heat. At temperatures above a million degrees Celsius, atoms lose many of their electrons. Heavier elements, including iron, can still retain a few, and those highly ionized atoms produce the unfamiliar lines. The corona’s light comes from gas hotter than the visible surface beneath it. Separate observations in the atmosphere notes reveal it. For a long time, the corona was studied from a distance. On April 28, 2021, Parker Solar Probe passed through a boundary where measurements showed that it had entered the magnetically dominated solar atmosphere. It sampled particles and magnetic fields directly. The phrase ‘touching the Sun’ describes that passage through the corona. There was no solid ground to land on. Farther out, escaping coronal material becomes the solar wind, carrying the Sun’s influence through the region we have been exploring.

title: High-gain antenna
description: The dish keeps the spacecraft in touch.
text: Each Voyager carries a 3.7-meter high-gain antenna. The dish concentrates radio communication into a narrow direction, carrying scientific measurements toward Earth and receiving commands from the ground. The attitude-control system maintains the spacecraft’s pointing. The dish is part of a spacecraft whose orientation must remain carefully controlled over enormous distances. This close view follows NASA’s artist model of the shared Voyager design. Its lighting makes the hardware visible; it is not a photograph taken beside either spacecraft.

title: Earth
description: The ground, seen from space.
text: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the largest of the four rocky inner planets. Its English name comes from a Germanic word meaning “the ground.” On December 7, 1972, the crew of Apollo 17, on their way to the Moon, photographed the Earth from the Mediterranean to the Antarctic ice cap, with almost the whole coastline of Africa in view. The photograph became known as the Blue Marble. The Earth shown here faces the same way. Its ocean, land and cloud shapes are an interpretation rather than a copy of that photograph.

title: Oceans
description: Mountains beneath the Atlantic.
text: The blue water west of Africa is the Atlantic Ocean. Beneath it runs the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, part of a mountain system that extends for nearly 65,000 kilometers around Earth. More than 90% of that system lies underwater. Along the ridge, tectonic plates move apart. Molten rock rises into the opening and cools into new ocean crust. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads at roughly two to five centimeters a year, gradually adding seafloor between the continents. Oceans cover about 71% of Earth. Much of the ground beneath them is hidden from this view, including the volcanic ridges where new crust forms.

title: Atmosphere
description: Most weather fits into a shallow layer.
text: Follow the pale blue curve around Earth. The atmosphere becomes thinner with height, gradually fading into space. Most familiar weather takes place near the bottom, in the troposphere, whose average height is only about 12 kilometers. It reaches higher over the equator and is shallower over the poles. The white cloud bands belong mainly to this lowest layer. Above them, the stratosphere contains the ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun. Farther up, the International Space Station travels through the extremely thin air of the thermosphere. The visible blue edge gives us a sense of the atmosphere, while its outer reaches extend well beyond that narrow band.

title: ISS
description: Sixteen sunrises in a day.
text: The station’s rectangular solar wings supply electrical power to its living and working spaces. This small outpost circles Earth about once every 90 minutes, giving its crew roughly 16 sunrises and sunsets in 24 hours. Inside, a released object floats beside an astronaut because both are falling with the station. Earth’s gravity keeps pulling them inward, while their sideways motion carries them around the planet. This continuous free fall produces the condition called microgravity. Bodies adapt to that environment. Muscles and bones do less work supporting a person’s weight, so astronauts exercise for at least two hours a day to help limit the resulting losses.

title: The Moon
description: Why one face keeps returning.
text: The familiar dark and light regions stay on the side of the Moon that faces Earth. The Moon turns once on its axis in the same time that it completes one orbit around us. This is synchronous rotation, also called tidal locking. Over time, Earth’s gravity deformed the rotating Moon. Friction within the changing shape dissipated energy and slowed its spin until rotation and orbit became synchronized. Sunlight still moves across both hemispheres. The far side has day and night, just as the near side does. The phases we see show how much of the sunlit half is facing us. Across the real gap between Earth and the Moon, about 30 Earth-sized planets would fit.

title: Lava plains
description: The dark plains were once lava.
text: Look at the broad dark areas between the lighter highlands. These are maria, Latin for seas. Ancient lava spread into large impact basins and cooled into plains of basalt. Basalt reflects less sunlight than the rocks in the surrounding highlands. The difference in brightness tells us something about the surface itself. These patches keep their character as the Sun moves across them, while the line between lunar day and night changes with the phases. The Moon as a whole reflects only about a tenth of the sunlight that reaches it. Much of its surface is dark gray. Its closeness to Earth allows that modest amount of reflected light to make a full Moon bright enough to cast shadows.

title: Craters
description: An old surface keeps the impacts.
text: The round depressions in the highlands record collisions with objects traveling through space. The Moon’s sparse atmosphere offers little protection, and a large impact can excavate a crater far wider than the object that made it. On Earth, water and wind wear down craters, while plate tectonics reshapes and recycles the surface. Lunar craters can remain recognizable for billions of years. Later impacts and the solar wind gradually alter them, so even a relatively fresh-looking crater may be hundreds of millions of years old. The repeated bombardment also breaks rock into smaller fragments and fine dust. This loose covering is regolith. Both the craters and the material around them preserve evidence of the collisions that shaped the Moon.

title: Mars
description: Rust carried across a planet.
text: Mars owes much of its reddish color to oxidized iron minerals in its dust. Over billions of years, erosion broke down iron-bearing material, and winds spread the fine grains across the planet. That dust also holds clues to earlier conditions. A 2025 study compared spacecraft observations with laboratory-made Mars dust and found a close match with ferrihydrite, a water-bearing form of iron oxide. Ferrihydrite commonly forms in cool water. The result suggests that some of the material responsible for Mars’s familiar color formed during a much wetter period, before winds spread it across the surface.

title: Olympus Mons
description: A mountain built by flowing lava.
text: The broad rise to the left of the other volcanoes is Olympus Mons. Overlapping lava flows built this shield volcano, which spans about 600 kilometers. Its slopes are gentle, with a steep scarp around the outer edge. The depressions at its summit are calderas. As underground magma chambers emptied, the ground above collapsed. Later eruptions and collapses produced overlapping depressions. Orbital images let scientists read the order of events. A lava flow that covers another must be younger. The mountain preserves many such crossings, so its surface records repeated episodes of building and collapse.

title: Valles Marineris
description: A canyon opened by a stretching crust.
text: The long broken band across the lower part of the globe is Valles Marineris, a canyon system about 4,000 kilometers long. Its connected troughs extend east from the Tharsis volcanic region. Scientists think the crust stretched and fractured as the neighboring volcanic plateau rose. Parts of the ground dropped, opening deep troughs. Erosion later widened and reshaped them. Some canyon walls have collapsed in enormous landslides. Orbital images show debris spread below the slopes, together with layers and dark deposits on the canyon floor. The outline we see brings together several processes acting over a long time.

title: North polar cap
description: Ice that changes with the seasons.
text: The pale patch near the northern limb marks the north polar cap. A core of water ice persists through the northern summer. In winter, a wider seasonal covering of carbon dioxide frost and ice grows around it. As sunlight returns, carbon dioxide ice changes directly into gas, a process called sublimation. The bright area retreats and exposes darker terrain, including a ring of sand dunes. At the edges, spacecraft have photographed layers containing different mixtures of ice and dust. These deposits preserve changes in the Martian climate. The small white patch in this view is the top of a much longer record.

title: Jupiter
description: A world with nowhere to land.
text: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system, about eleven times as wide as Earth. The striped globe shows its upper clouds. Beneath them lies an enormous body made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Pressure and temperature rise with depth, compressing hydrogen into liquid. There is no solid surface where a spacecraft could land. Farther inside, the pressure is great enough for hydrogen to conduct electricity like a metal. Juno’s measurements suggest that even the core has an indistinct boundary. Heavier material appears partly mixed into the surrounding hydrogen, giving Jupiter what researchers call a dilute core.

title: Cloud bands
description: Winds that reach deep into Jupiter.
text: The pale stripes are zones; the darker stripes are belts. They follow Jupiter’s eastward and westward winds. Along their boundaries, the clouds curl into smaller swirls and eddies. Juno measured tiny variations in Jupiter’s gravity to investigate how far these flows extend. The results showed that the winds reach roughly 3,000 kilometers below the cloud tops, carrying a substantial part of the planet’s atmosphere with them. Jupiter turns once in about ten hours. Its rapid rotation helps organize the winds into the long bands visible here. Their familiar pattern is the outward sign of motion extending far below what a camera can see.

title: Great Red Spot
description: A storm that changes shape.
text: The rusty oval below Jupiter’s equator is the Great Red Spot. It is an anticyclone, a storm circulating around a region of high pressure, held between two strong jet streams. Astronomers have monitored it for more than 150 years. Hubble observations from December 2023 to March 2024 showed the storm stretching and squeezing over a roughly 90-day cycle. Its shape, brightness and motion changed together. Those observations did not establish what caused the oscillation. The oval in this Hubble image represents a changing weather system. Comparing images taken at different times lets researchers follow its behavior, including the long-term shrinking recorded by Hubble.

title: Io
description: A moon heated by its orbit.
text: Io’s yellow and rusty surface carries sulfur-rich deposits and dark volcanic areas. Eruptions repeatedly cover older ground, making this small rocky moon the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Jupiter pulls strongly on Io, while Europa and Ganymede repeatedly disturb its orbit. The resulting slightly elliptical path makes Jupiter’s tidal pull vary. Io flexes as it travels, and this movement generates heat inside the moon. That heat feeds volcanic activity. Fresh flows and deposits can cover impact craters, continually changing the surface. The mottled colors in this view belong to a landscape that volcanic activity continually renews.

title: Europa
description: Clues to an ocean under the ice.
text: The pale surface of Europa is water ice crossed by reddish-brown fractures. Its relatively small number of impact craters suggests that the surface has been renewed over geological time. A particularly strong clue to what lies below came from the Galileo spacecraft. It measured a magnetic response around Europa as Jupiter’s magnetic field swept past. Scientists interpret that response as evidence for an electrically conducting layer beneath the ice, most plausibly a global ocean of salty water. The evidence for an ocean is strong, but the ocean itself has not been directly observed. The cracked shell visible here is the boundary through which scientists investigate that hidden interior.

title: Saturn
description: A short day, a long year.
text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest. Hydrogen and helium make up most of the planet. The soft bands in the image show clouds above deeper layers of gas and liquid, with no solid surface where a visitor could stand. The planet turns once in about eleven hours. That rapid rotation gives it an equatorial bulge and visibly flattened poles. A year passes much more slowly: Saturn takes about 29 Earth years to complete one orbit of the Sun. Its tilted axis also gives it seasons. Each lasts for years, changing how sunlight falls across the planet and its rings.

title: Rings
description: The shape that puzzled Galileo.
text: When Galileo turned his telescope toward Saturn in 1610, he saw a central body with two smaller shapes beside it. The instrument could not resolve the rings. Other observers drew handles, and at times the side features seemed to vanish as the rings turned edge-on to Earth. In the 1650s, Christiaan Huygens worked out that a thin, flat ring surrounded the planet without touching it. He published the explanation in Systema Saturnium in 1659. We now know that the rings contain countless separate particles, mostly water ice. Each follows its own orbit around Saturn. From a distance those moving pieces form the broad, continuous-looking bands in the image.

title: Cassini Division
description: What the dark band contains.
text: The dark lane separates the bright B ring from the outer A ring. Called the Cassini Division, it is roughly 4,800 kilometers wide. Voyager’s close views revealed distinct ringlets inside the region that looks like a gap from Earth. The moon Mimas helps shape its inner boundary. Near the outer edge of the B ring, particles complete about two orbits for each orbit of Mimas. The moon’s repeated gravitational tugs build up, helping maintain the sharp edge. The dark band in this painting simplifies that fine structure. Looking closer with a spacecraft turns an apparently empty strip into another part of the ring system.

title: Titan
description: Rain beneath an orange haze.
text: Titan’s orange haze hides the surface beneath a dense atmosphere made mostly of nitrogen. High above the ground, sunlight and energetic particles break apart nitrogen and methane molecules. Their fragments recombine into compounds that help form the haze. Below it, methane and ethane collect in lakes and seas. Methane can fall as rain and flow through channels. At Titan’s bitterly cold temperatures, water ice forms hard ground while these other substances can remain liquid. On January 14, 2005, ESA’s Huygens probe descended through the atmosphere and landed. The moon that looks featureless in visible light became a landscape that a camera could show from the ground.

title: Enceladus
description: An ocean that sends samples into space.
text: Enceladus is only about 500 kilometers across. Its bright ice reflects much of the sunlight that reaches it. Near the south pole, long fractures release jets of water vapor and icy particles into space. Cassini flew through the plume and sampled material from within the moon. Measurements of gravity and the moon’s slight wobble also support a global ocean beneath the frozen shell. Some of the expelled ice falls back onto Enceladus, refreshing its bright surface. Some escapes into Saturn’s faint E ring, beyond the main rings shown here. The pale moon and the surrounding ring system exchange material.

title: Uranus
description: The color of an ice giant.
text: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Its atmosphere contains mostly hydrogen and helium, with a small amount of methane. Methane absorbs red light from the sunlight passing through the atmosphere, giving the planet its blue-green appearance. The name ice giant refers to materials such as water, ammonia and methane in its interior. Models include hot, dense fluids beneath the atmosphere. There is no solid surface on which a spacecraft could land. Voyager 2 passed Uranus on January 24, 1986. Much of our close-range knowledge of the planet and its moons comes from that brief encounter.

title: Sideways spin
description: Seasons on a tilted world.
text: Uranus is tipped almost onto its side. Its rotation axis is tilted about 98 degrees, measured from a line perpendicular to its orbit. The rings lie close to its equatorial plane and share the planet’s unusual orientation. A rotation takes about seventeen hours, while one journey around the Sun takes 84 Earth years. During that long year, the poles experience extended periods of continuous daylight and darkness, producing extreme seasonal changes. A large collision early in the planet’s history is one proposed explanation for the tilt. The cause has not been established.

title: Rings
description: Found in a star’s interrupted light.
text: On March 10, 1977, astronomers watched Uranus pass in front of a distant star. They expected the event to reveal information about the planet’s atmosphere. Before the star disappeared behind Uranus, its light briefly faded several times. Similar dips followed after it reappeared. The interruptions came from narrow rings crossing the line of sight. The repeating pattern revealed material on both sides of the planet, even though the rings themselves were difficult to distinguish in its glare. Voyager 2 later examined the ring system at close range. Stronger contrast makes the few ring traces in this watercolor easier to explore.

title: Miranda
description: Different histories on one small moon.
text: Miranda is only about 500 kilometers across, yet its surface holds sharply different kinds of terrain. In Voyager 2’s images, heavily cratered ground meets regions of grooves and ridges along abrupt boundaries. The angled bright marking and the banded lower region in this Voyager mosaic. The older cratered areas and younger, reshaped terrain show that the moon has experienced different episodes of geological activity. How those changes happened remains uncertain. Gerard Kuiper discovered Miranda in 1948. Its name comes from Prospero’s daughter in Shakespeare’s The Tempest, one of several literary names among Uranus’s moons.

title: Neptune
description: A planet found through another planet’s orbit.
text: Uranus did not follow quite the orbit astronomers had calculated. Urbain Le Verrier investigated whether the gravity of an unseen planet could account for the difference and calculated where that planet might be. He sent his prediction to Johann Gottfried Galle in Berlin. In 1846, Galle found Neptune on the first night of searching. The journey from Uranus to Neptune follows a connection that helped astronomers discover the outer planet. Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun, about thirty times farther out than Earth. One orbit takes roughly 165 Earth years. Its visible globe is atmosphere; this ice giant has no solid surface on which to land.

title: Blue-green light
description: Why the familiar blue was too strong.
text: Neptune and Uranus both have a blue-green appearance. Methane in their atmospheres absorbs red light. The deep royal blue familiar from many Neptune pictures owes much to choices in processing the spacecraft images. Voyager cameras recorded separate images through different filters. Combining them required choices about color balance and contrast. Stronger contrast helped reveal Neptune’s clouds, but some widely circulated versions made the planet look much bluer. A 2024 study used telescope spectra to rebalance the images. It found that the two planets are much closer in color, with Neptune slightly bluer. This view uses the earlier Voyager color processing, whose stronger blue and contrast help reveal the clouds.

title: Great Dark Spot
description: A storm that disappeared.
text: Voyager 2 photographed the Great Dark Spot in Neptune’s southern hemisphere in 1989. The dark oval and thin bright clouds beside it in this image belong to that encounter. The white clouds contain methane ice. When Hubble observed Neptune in 1994, that spot had vanished. Later observations recorded other dark storms appearing and changing. A picture of Neptune captures weather at a particular time. By comparing repeated images, astronomers can follow the storms’ growth and motion. The oval here belongs to the Voyager era. It is not a view of Neptune’s present weather.

title: Triton
description: An orbit that points to capture.
text: Triton travels around Neptune in the opposite direction to the planet’s rotation. It is the only large moon in the solar system with this kind of retrograde orbit. That unusual motion is a major clue to its past. Scientists think Neptune captured Triton from a separate orbit around the Sun. A former home among the icy bodies of the Kuiper Belt would help explain its similarities to Pluto. Capture is an interpretation of the evidence. About 2,700 kilometers across, Triton has an icy surface and a thin atmosphere made mostly of nitrogen. The broad pale southern region in this view follows the polar cap photographed by Voyager 2. The moon is enlarged here so its surface can be explored.

title: Dark streaks
description: Traces carried by the wind.
text: The small dark marks on Triton’s pale southern ice are deposits recorded in Voyager images. Scientists interpret many of these streaks as fine material carried downwind from geyser-like plumes. In 1989, Voyager 2 photographed active plumes rising about eight kilometers above Triton. Their dark particles spread sideways through the thin atmosphere. The streaks on the ground preserve another part of that activity. One proposed mechanism involves sunlight warming material beneath nitrogen ice. Trapped gas builds pressure and escapes through openings, carrying particles with it. The driving mechanism remains under investigation. This mosaic shows the surface deposits; active plumes are not resolved in this view.

title: Pluto
description: A world among the Kuiper Belt’s icy bodies.
text: Pluto belongs to the Kuiper Belt, a region of icy bodies beyond Neptune. After its discovery in 1930, it was counted as the ninth planet for more than seventy years. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union classified it as a dwarf planet. Pluto circles the Sun and its gravity has made it nearly round. It does not meet the additional planetary criterion of having cleared its orbital neighborhood. New Horizons flew past in July 2015, revealing a landscape of glaciers and mountains. This view follows the hemisphere seen during that encounter, including the broad bright region named Tombaugh Regio, often called Pluto’s heart. This New Horizons image combines blue, red and infrared observations from July 14, 2015. Its colors are enhanced to reveal differences across the surface. The camera stays on the same observation when you approach the bright plain.

title: Sputnik Planitia
description: Ice that slowly renews its surface.
text: The smooth left lobe of Pluto’s bright heart is Sputnik Planitia. Nitrogen ice fills this broad basin. Its pale surface contrasts with the darker, rougher terrain along its western edge. New Horizons photographed broad cells across parts of the plain. Scientists compared their shapes with computer models and found that slow convection in solid nitrogen ice could produce the pattern. Warmer ice rises from below, spreads and cools, then sinks near the cell boundaries. This movement can replace older surface material and help explain why the plain has so few impact craters. The closer view uses the same New Horizons image as the whole globe; fine patterns become easier to distinguish as the native-resolution image loads.

title: Charon
description: The moon first seen as a moving bulge.
text: In 1978, James Christy noticed that some telescope images of Pluto looked stretched. The bulge changed position in a repeating cycle. Archived images showed it too, and further observations confirmed a large moon. Charon is about half Pluto’s diameter. The two worlds keep the same faces toward each other, a state called mutual tidal locking. Charon’s orbit and each world’s rotation take about 6.4 Earth days. From a place on Pluto facing Charon, the moon stays in the same part of the sky. The two globe portraits here show terrain photographed by New Horizons, arranged separately for exploration. The image was taken on July 14, 2015. Its enhanced colors emphasize differences in surface properties, including the reddish northern polar region. Pluto and Charon remain in fixed places in this illustrative arrangement as you travel between them.

title: Reddish pole
description: Material that may have come from Pluto.
text: Charon is mostly gray, but its northern polar region has a reddish-brown tint. New Horizons images and models of the moon’s long seasons led researchers to an explanation involving its companion. In this model, methane escaping from Pluto reaches Charon and freezes at the winter pole. Radiation alters the trapped material into heavier compounds. When sunlight returns, much of the methane escapes again, while less volatile products remain. Further irradiation can produce reddish organic material called tholins. The model agrees with the observed color pattern; it reconstructs a process that the spacecraft could not watch over an entire seasonal cycle.

title: Venus
description: A familiar size, a very different climate.
text: Venus is the second planet from the Sun. At about 12,100 kilometers across, it is only a little smaller than Earth. Both are rocky worlds, but their atmospheres have followed very different histories. Venus’s thick atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide. It traps enough heat to make the surface about 465°C, hotter than Mercury’s average surface despite being farther from the Sun. Surface pressure is roughly ninety times the pressure at sea level on Earth. The pale globe here shows the cloud cover. The rocky ground and its extreme conditions are hidden beneath it.

title: Acid clouds
description: Clouds that circle faster than the world below.
text: Venus’s clouds contain tiny droplets of sulfuric acid. They reflect much of the sunlight that reaches them, helping Venus appear so bright in Earth’s sky. In visible light, the cloud cover looks nearly featureless. Ultraviolet images reveal sweeping patterns. The upper clouds can circle the planet in roughly four to five Earth days, while the solid world takes about 243 days to turn once. This fast atmospheric circulation is called superrotation. This Mariner 10 composite combines orange and ultraviolet observations from February 1974. Its colors are assigned to reveal atmospheric differences. They mark an atmosphere that keeps changing; no surface geography is visible through them.

title: Slow spin
description: Two different ways to count a day.
text: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once relative to the distant stars. Its year, one orbit of the Sun, lasts about 225 Earth days. The planet completes an orbit before it finishes that single turn. It also turns in the opposite direction to most planets. If the clouds allowed a view of the Sun from the surface, it would rise in the west and set in the east. A solar day measures the interval from one noon to the next. Venus’s slow backward rotation combines with its orbital motion to make that interval about 117 Earth days. The rotation period and the solar day measure different things.

title: Phases
description: Changing light helped reveal an orbit.
text: Sunlight illuminates half of Venus. From Earth, we see different portions of that sunlit half as the two planets move around the Sun. Through a telescope, Venus changes from a thin crescent to a nearly full disk, growing smaller in apparent size as it moves farther away. Galileo began observing these phases in 1610. The nearly full phases contradicted the traditional Ptolemaic arrangement, which kept Venus between Earth and the Sun and could produce only a narrow range of crescents. The observations supported an orbit around the Sun. Tycho Brahe’s alternative system also accommodated them, so the phases alone did not settle every question about Earth’s motion. The light and shadow here are a chosen view, rather than Venus’s current appearance from Earth.

title: Magellan
description: A way to map the ground beneath the clouds.
text: Magellan reached Venus in 1990. Its large dish sent radar signals through the cloud cover and received their echoes from the ground. The measurements revealed mountains, lava plains and craters beneath the opaque atmosphere. By the end of its third mapping cycle, the mission had covered about 98 percent of the surface. The spacecraft incorporated spare hardware left over from earlier missions. It ended its work in 1994, when controllers sent it into the atmosphere. The cloud view in this journey does not show Magellan; this note describes the mission that mapped the hidden ground. Its images kept yielding discoveries. In a study published in 2023, researchers compared observations from February and October 1991 and found a vent near Maat Mons had changed shape and doubled in area. Modeling supported a volcanic eruption as the cause.

title: Mercury
description: A small world with a marked surface.
text: Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets, only a little larger than our Moon. It orbits closest to the Sun. Its gray-brown surface records impacts, with bright streaks spreading from some younger craters. Those rays are crushed rock thrown out during impacts. Freshly exposed material reflects more light. The broad pale area higher on the globe is Caloris, a much older impact basin. Sunlit ground can reach about 430°C, while nighttime temperatures can fall to about −180°C. Mercury’s extremely thin exosphere cannot hold heat the way a substantial atmosphere can. Venus remains the hotter planet.

title: Caloris Basin
description: A basin filled after the collision.
text: The broad pale patch near the upper right represents Caloris Basin, roughly 1,500 kilometers across. An enormous impact excavated it, and lava later flooded its floor. Smaller impacts then punched through those volcanic plains. Some excavated darker material from below. The basin holds a sequence of events that geologists can read from which features cut through others. MESSENGER’s color images help distinguish surface materials. Some published views enhance those differences strongly. This MESSENGER mosaic uses infrared, far-red and violet observations in assigned color channels, revealing subtle compositional differences. The close view stays within that same mosaic.

title: A long day
description: One solar day lasts two Mercury years.
text: Mercury circles the Sun in about 88 Earth days and turns once on its axis in about 59. Together, these motions make a complete sunrise-to-sunrise cycle last about 176 Earth days. Its speed also changes along its elongated orbit. Near the closest approach to the Sun, the Sun’s apparent movement can briefly reverse. From some places, a sunrise can be followed by a sunset and another sunrise. The shaded edge in this observation is the boundary between day and night in this chosen view. It does not divide a permanently lit face from a permanently dark one.

title: Polar shadows
description: Some crater floors never receive sunlight.
text: Near Mercury’s poles, parts of deep craters remain in permanent shadow. These cold places can preserve water ice even while sunlit ground elsewhere becomes extremely hot. Earth-based radar first found unusually reflective polar deposits. MESSENGER added measurements of hydrogen and models of the temperatures, providing strong evidence for water ice. A darker insulating layer covers some deposits. This label marks the polar region. This observation does not resolve the individual deposits hidden inside those small, shadowed craters; there is no broad white ice cap.

title: The Sun
description: The light reaches every world here.
text: The Sun’s gravity keeps the planets in orbit. Deep inside it, hydrogen fuses into helium, releasing the energy that eventually leaves as sunlight. Approach the disk to explore its visible surface and dark sunspots. Read “What the light told us” for the history of these observations, or open the atmosphere notes for separate views of prominences and the corona. The main view is an SDO/HMI visible-light observation from February 2011, with a display color added by NASA. Sunlight is white.

title: The asteroid belt
description: Most of the belt is empty space.
text: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Its worlds follow their own paths around the Sun, usually separated by enormous stretches of space. A spacecraft can cross the region with little chance of passing close to an asteroid. These bodies preserve material from the early Solar System. As Jupiter grew, its gravity disturbed motion in this region, helping prevent a planet from assembling and making collisions more destructive. Those collisions have continued to reshape the belt. Ceres and Vesta appear together here as separate enlarged portraits. Their spacing in this arrangement helps exploration; it does not show how close they are in space.

title: Ceres
description: A point of light became a world.
text: Giuseppe Piazzi discovered Ceres in 1801. This dwarf planet is the largest body in the asteroid belt, about 950 kilometers across. Dawn entered orbit in 2015. Its close views turned a distant point into a cratered landscape. This Dawn mosaic centers on Occator, the crater with the small pale deposits. Those bright patches became one of the mission’s most revealing clues. Open their label to see how measurements of reflected light and gravity helped scientists investigate what lies beneath the surface.

title: Bright salts
description: Salt records the movement of water.
text: Occator is about 92 kilometers wide. Its brightest deposits contain sodium carbonate, a salt. Briny liquid reached the surface; as the water escaped into space, reflective minerals remained. Dawn measured the composition of the deposits from reflected light. Later close passes also revealed variations in gravity. Together with geological models, the observations indicate that some brine came from a deep reservoir below the crater. The pale patches in this close view are those deposits. They shine by reflecting sunlight. The reservoir itself is hidden beneath the ground.

title: Vesta
description: Some meteorites bring pieces of this world.
text: Vesta’s uneven outline and grooved terrain bear traces of enormous impacts. Two overlapping basins occupy its southern region. The younger one, Rheasilvia, is roughly 500 kilometers across, comparable to Vesta’s own size. Dawn’s measurements connected this distant surface with rocks already held in laboratories on Earth. The spacecraft found a close match between Vesta’s mineral composition and a group of meteorites called howardites, eucrites and diogenites. The evidence strongly supports Vesta as their source. Impacts can eject fragments into space. Some eventually cross Earth’s orbit and survive the fall through its atmosphere. These samples let researchers study parts of Vesta directly, alongside the spacecraft observations. This view uses a Dawn mosaic. Its southern relief and grooves record a history of immense impacts.

title: The Kuiper Belt
description: Pluto belongs to a much larger population.
text: The main Kuiper Belt stretches from near Neptune’s orbit, about 30 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, to roughly 50 times that distance. It contains icy remnants of the material from which the planets formed. Pluto is one of its members. The objects’ orbits preserve clues to their history. Pluto follows a repeating rhythm with Neptune, completing two orbits while Neptune completes three. Arrokoth belongs to the cold classical population, whose relatively round, lightly tilted orbits have been less disturbed. Here “cold” describes the motion of those orbits. Arrokoth’s quiet orbital history helps explain why it can preserve evidence from the Solar System’s beginnings. This view approaches one small member of this enormous region. The route compresses distances and does not represent the objects’ orbital positions.

title: Arrokoth
description: The next close encounter after Pluto.
text: Arrokoth is about 35 kilometers long and follows an orbit roughly 45 times Earth’s distance from the Sun. New Horizons revealed its two joined lobes during the flyby on January 1, 2019. The same spacecraft had flown past Pluto on July 14, 2015. It continued into the Kuiper Belt and sent back images of this much smaller world. Views from different angles helped researchers reconstruct its three-dimensional shape, including the flattened larger lobe. This New Horizons composite combines enhanced-color data with higher-resolution panchromatic imagery. The wide and close views use the same observation, preserving the outline, pale neck and surface features. Image credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute/Roman Tkachenko.

title: The neck
description: The joined lobes record a gentle merger.
text: The pale curved strip lies at the narrow connection between Arrokoth’s lobes. Together, the two parts form a contact binary: bodies that came together and remained joined. Their flattened shapes and closely aligned axes support a gentle merger. Researchers interpret these features as evidence that the two lobes formed within the same collapsing cloud of particles, then approached each other slowly. The encounter itself was not observed. This account comes from comparing the surviving shape with models of how small bodies assemble. The relatively intact lobes make Arrokoth a useful record of an early stage in planet formation.

title: Reddish surface
description: The color carries clues to surface chemistry.
text: New Horizons measured the wavelengths of light reflected by Arrokoth. Its spectrum contains signatures of frozen methanol. The surface is reddish across both lobes, with modest local differences. Researchers interpret the red color as evidence of complex organic material, probably altered or produced as radiation acts on simpler molecules. The exact mixture remains uncertain. In chemistry, “organic” refers to carbon-containing compounds; the term alone makes no claim about life. This spacecraft composite uses enhanced color. Its brightness helps reveal the shape; the close view cannot identify individual molecules by sight. Arrokoth reflects only a small fraction of the sunlight that reaches it.

title: Voyager 1
description: Titan helped determine the route.
text: Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, after Voyager 2. Its faster route carried it past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. At Saturn, a close encounter with Titan was a priority. The chosen path took Voyager 1 north of the plane in which most planets orbit. Its planetary tour ended there, while Voyager 2 continued toward Uranus and Neptune. The broad dish in this NASA model is its 3.7-meter high-gain antenna. The spacecraft’s attitude-control system keeps it pointed toward Earth so radio signals can carry observations home and commands back out. The two spacecraft have the same basic design. Both are shown using the same NASA model in separate regions of this journey. The camera crosses empty space between their paths; positions and distances are illustrative.

title: Voyager 2
description: One spacecraft visited all four giant planets.
text: Voyager 2 launched on August 20, 1977. It passed Jupiter in 1979, Saturn in 1981, Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. The planets’ arrangement allowed a sequence of gravity assists. Each encounter changed the spacecraft’s motion relative to the Sun and set up the next destination. At Saturn, its path preserved the onward route to Uranus. Voyager 2 supplied the close views of Neptune and Triton used in this journey. After the Neptune encounter, it headed south of the planets’ orbital plane, taking a different path into interstellar space from Voyager 1. Voyager 2 appears alone here. Voyager 1 is far away in another direction; the camera travels through empty space before reaching it.

title: Beyond the solar wind
description: Interstellar space begins beyond the heliopause.
text: The solar wind is a flow of charged particles from the Sun. It forms a large surrounding region called the heliosphere. At its outer boundary, the heliopause, the outward solar wind meets the interstellar environment. Voyager 1 crossed this boundary on August 25, 2012. Voyager 2 crossed on November 5, 2018. Scientists identified the transitions through instrument measurements. At Voyager 2, the measured solar-wind flow dropped sharply, alongside changes in energetic particles. The Sun’s gravity reaches much farther. The Oort Cloud is a proposed distant reservoir of icy bodies, inferred from comet orbits, well beyond either Voyager. Crossing the heliopause therefore marks a change in the surrounding plasma; it does not put a spacecraft beyond every boundary used for the Solar System. There is no visible wall here. The dark background leaves the boundary to its measurements.

title: Golden Record
description: Sounds and pictures from Earth travel with them.
text: Each Voyager carries a 30-centimeter gold-plated copper record beneath a protective aluminum cover. The small gold circle on the equipment body marks its location in this NASA model. Planetary scientist Carl Sagan of Cornell University chaired the committee that selected the contents. Alongside music and natural sounds, the records hold greetings in 55 languages, including Turkish, and 115 encoded images. Linda Salzman Sagan organized the spoken greetings. The cover supplies symbolic instructions for playing the record and reconstructing its images. A cartridge and needle travel with it. Hearing the message would require someone to encounter the spacecraft and work out how to read it. The cover also gives a return address.
